paragraphs.text: Among the buildings in the dreary town of Mudfog was a workhouse, where the poor were housed and many of them were worked to death. Oliver Twist was born in this dismal place, but for a few minutes it was doubtful he would survive.
At last he breathed, sneezed, and let out a loud wail. Hearing this, a young woman raised her head feebly from her pillow. "Let me see the child and die."
"Oh, you must not talk about dying yet," said the doctor who had attended the birth.
"Bless her heart, no," said the old pauper woman who was serving as nurse. "Think about being a mother to your new baby, dear."
The young mother stretched out her hand toward the child. The doctor deposited the baby in her arms. She imprinted her cold lips passionately on his forehead, shuddered, and died.
"It's all over," said the doctor. "She was a nice-looking girl. Where did she come from?"
"She was brought here last night," replied the old woman. "She was found lying in the street. But where she came from or where she was going, nobody knows."
The doctor leaned over the body. "The same old story." He shook his head. "No wedding ring. Well, good night. If the child cries, give it a little gruel."
Wrapped in an old calico blanket, Oliver cried lustily. If he had known he was a workhouse orphan, he would have cried even louder.

When Oliver was about eight months old, he was sent to a branch workhouse—a farm run by an elderly woman. Mrs. Mann was a woman of wisdom and experience. She knew what was good for the children under her care, and she knew what was good for her. So she took the greater part of their weekly stipends for her own use and fed the children as little as possible.

By his tenth birthday, Oliver was a pale child, small for his age and quite thin. But luckily nature had planted a good, sturdy spirit in Oliver's heart. For he was spending his birthday locked in the coal cellar with two other orphans for daring to be hungry.
Mrs. Mann looked out the window and saw a large, fat man fumbling with the latch on the front gate.
"The parish officer is here!" she cried to her servant. "Take Oliver and those two brats upstairs and wash them right away before Mr. Bumble sees them!"
"Why is this gate locked?" The man rattled the gate as Mrs. Mann appeared. "You're keeping a parish officer waiting. And I am here on official business!"
"How delightful to see you, Mr. Bumble!" Mrs. Mann opened the gate. "I was just telling the dear children, who are so fond of you, that you're here."
Mrs. Mann ushered him into the parlor, where he removed his hat, and they sat down.
"Oliver Twist is ten years old today," said Mr. Bumble.
"Bless him," interrupted Mrs. Mann.
"And despite offering a reward of ten pounds—later increased to twenty pounds—the parish has never been able to discover the names of his parents."
"Then how did he get a name?"

Mr. Bumble drew himself up with pride. "I name all the orphans in alphabetical order. The last was Swubble, then Twist, then Unwin. But returning to business, Oliver is too old to remain here. I've come myself to take him back to the workhouse, so let me see him at once."
Mrs. Mann went to fetch Oliver.
"Make a bow to the gentleman, Oliver," she said when they returned.
Oliver bowed.
"Very good, Oliver. Now come along with me." And with that, Mr. Bumble put on his hat and bade the surprised Mrs. Mann good day.
Mr. Bumble walked quickly down the road with little Oliver clutching his coat cuff.
"Are we nearly there?" Oliver gasped every quarter mile.
"Not yet," Mr. Bumble said with growing impatience.
At last they arrived at a huge, prison-like building.
"You've come here to be taught a useful trade," said Mr. Bumble. "Starting tomorrow morning at six o'clock, you'll pick apart old ropes so they can be reused."
Oliver barely had time to look around before he was hurried away to receive his dreary uniform. That night he sobbed himself to sleep on a hard bed in a room full of other boys.

Three months passed. The board running the workhouse decided that too many poor people were taking advantage of its services. To reduce the number of paupers, they drastically reduced the amount of food.

Now each boy was allowed only one small bowl of gruel. The boys were fed in a great stone hall. Once a day, the master of the workhouse, assisted by two women, ladled out the gruel from a large copper pot.
"If I don't get more to eat," said a new boy, "I might have to eat one of you." He glared at the other boys with a wild, hungry look in his eyes, frightening them.
That night the boys decided that someone had to ask the master for more food. They drew lots, and Oliver got the job.

The next evening the boys arrived in the dining hall. They stood in line while the master filled their bowls. Then they sat down, and the gruel quickly disappeared. The boys whispered to each other and winked at Oliver.
Oliver was desperate with hunger and reckless with misery. He rose from the table and walked toward the master.
"Please, sir." Oliver held up his bowl. "I want some more."
The master aimed a blow at Oliver's head with his ladle. "Call Mr. Bumble!"
The parish officer came running from a board meeting, and when he heard Oliver's request, he ran right back.
"I beg your pardon, Mr. Limbkins," Mr. Bumble said to the head of the board. "Oliver Twist has asked for more food."
There was horror on every face in the room.
"For more ?" said Mr. Limbkins. "Compose yourself, Bumble, and answer me. Do I understand he asked for more after he'd eaten the amount allotted to him?"
"He did, sir," replied Mr. Bumble.
"That boy will come to a bad end." Mr. Limbkins shook his head, and no one disagreed.

Oliver was instantly locked up. The next morning a notice was posted on the workhouse gate, offering five pounds to anyone who wanted an apprentice. In other words, they were looking for anyone who would take Oliver Twist off the hands of the parish.

Oliver was confined to a dark and lonely room for a week after he had dared to ask for more gruel. No one responded to the notice offering him as an apprentice. The workhouse board began to think about sending him to sea to work as a cabin boy.
The board members sent Mr. Bumble out to make some inquiries to ship captains. He was just returning to the workhouse when he met the village undertaker, Mr. Sowerberry, at the gate.
"I've come for the two women who died last night," said Mr. Sowerberry as he cordially stepped forward and shook Mr. Bumble's hand.
"You'll make a fortune when the board pays you, Mr. Sowerberry," said Mr. Bumble.
The undertaker shook his head. "The amount paid by the board for the paupers' coffins is very small."
"So are the coffins!"
Mr. Bumble allowed himself only a smile because he was an important official. But Mr. Sowerberry was very amused by the joke and laughed for a long time.
"Well, Mr. Bumble," he said at last, "there's no denying that the coffins are somewhat narrower since you started feeding the paupers less."

That reminded the parish officer of Oliver. "You don't know anybody who wants an apprentice, do you?" Mr. Bumble raised his cane to the notice on the gate and gave three raps on the words "Five Pounds."
"That's the very thing I wanted to speak to you about! I pay so much in taxes to support the poor, I have a right to get a lot out of them. So I'll take the boy myself."

Mr. Bumble grasped the undertaker by the arm and hurried him into the workhouse. Within five minutes the board decided that Oliver should go to Mr. Sowerberry immediately for a month's trial period. That evening Oliver was brought before the board and informed that he was to become an apprentice to the undertaker.
"And if you ever complain or come back to this workhouse again, you will be sent to sea," said Mr. Limbkins, the head of the board. "Do you understand, boy?"
Oliver nodded and showed no emotion.
"Oh, he's a hardened young rascal," said Mr. Limbkins as Oliver was led away by Mr. Bumble. The other board members nodded in agreement.
So Oliver pulled his cap over his eyes, picked up the small brown paper parcel that contained all his belongings, and once more attached himself to Mr. Bumble's coat cuff.

For some time Mr. Bumble drew Oliver along without noticing him. This was partly because the parish officer held his head high, as an important parish officer always should. And this was also because it was a windy day. Little Oliver was completely hidden by Mr. Bumble's coat whenever it blew open.
As they drew near their destination, however, Mr. Bumble thought he should make sure that the boy was ready for inspection by the undertaker.
"Oliver!" said Mr. Bumble.
"Yes, sir," replied Oliver in a low, tremulous voice.
"Pull that cap off your eyes and hold up your head."

Oliver immediately did what he was told. As he was pushing up his cap, a tear fell on his hand. And as Mr. Bumble gazed sternly upon him, another tear rolled down his cheek. It was followed by another and another. Oliver covered his face with both hands and wept.
Mr. Bumble glared at Oliver. "Well, of all the most ungrateful and worst-behaved boys that I have ever seen, Oliver, you are the—"
"No, no, sir." Oliver sobbed. "I will be good. Indeed, sir, I will. I'm a very little boy, sir, and it's so . . . so . . ."
"So what?" Mr. Bumble asked in amazement.
"So lonely, sir. So very lonely! Everybody hates me. Oh, please don't be angry with me!"

For a moment Mr. Bumble regarded Oliver with some astonishment. "Ahem . . . well, yes . . . ahem . . . oh, this troublesome cough," said the parish officer. He cleared his throat and managed to keep the tears from his own eyes.
"Now dry your eyes and be a good boy," he finally said to Oliver. He took Oliver's hand and they walked on in silence.
Mr. Sowerberry was busy making some entries in a ledger when they arrived at his shop.
"Here!" said Mr. Bumble. "I've brought the boy."
Oliver made a bow.
"Oh, that's the boy, is it?" The undertaker raised his candle to get a better view of Oliver. "Mrs. Sowerberry, will you have the goodness to come here a moment, my dear?"
Mrs. Sowerberry emerged from a little room behind the shop.
"My dear," said Mr. Sowerberry, "this is the boy from the workhouse that I told you about."
Oliver bowed again.
"Oh, my!" said the undertaker's wife. "He's very small."
"Yes, he is rather small," agreed Mr. Bumble. "But he'll grow."

"I daresay he will grow, once he starts eating our food and drink," said Mrs. Sowerberry. "I see no saving in employing workhouse children for they always cost more than they're worth. But men always think they know best. Get downstairs, little bag of bones."

With that, Mrs. Sowerberry opened a door and pushed Oliver down a steep flight of stairs to the kitchen. A servant girl was sitting in the kitchen, which was a damp, dark room just outside the cellar.

"Here, Charlotte," said Mrs. Sowerberry, who had followed Oliver downstairs. "Give this boy the cold meat scraps you were saving for the dog. That animal hasn't come home all day, so he'll have to do without. I'm sure this boy isn't too fussy to eat them. Are you, boy?"
Oliver's eyes lit up at the mention of meat. "Oh no, ma'am."
Charlotte set a plate of meat scraps before him, and Oliver gobbled up the dog's food.
In silent horror Mrs. Sowerberry watched Oliver eat. If he was this hungry now, how much would he eat when he was bigger?
"Well," she said when Oliver had finished his supper. "Are you done?"
Oliver looked around the kitchen. There was nothing more to eat within his reach. "Yes," he said.
"Then come with me." Mrs. Sowerberry picked up a dim and dirty lamp and led the way upstairs. "Your bed's under the counter. You don't mind sleeping among the coffins?"
Oliver hesitated on the stairs.
"Well, it doesn't matter whether you do or don't because you can't sleep anywhere else," said Mrs. Sowerberry. "Come on! Don't keep me here all night!"
Oliver meekly followed his new mistress upstairs.
"Open the door!"
The next morning Oliver woke up because someone was loudly kicking the front door of the undertaker's shop.
"Open the door!" cried the voice again.
"Yes, sir," replied Oliver, struggling into his clothes.
"Are you the new boy?" asked the voice through the keyhole.
"Yes, sir," replied Oliver.
"Then I'll beat you up when I get in, workhouse brat!" Having made this dreadful promise, the voice began to whistle.
Oliver turned the key with a trembling hand and opened the door. He glanced up and down the street. But all he could see was an older boy, sitting on a hitching post and eating a slice of bread.
"I beg your pardon, sir," Oliver said at last. "Did you knock?"
"I kicked."
"Did you want a coffin, sir?" Oliver innocently inquired.
"You'll be wanting a coffin soon if you keep this up. You don't know who I am, do you?" The boy jumped down from the post.
"No, sir."
"I'm Mister Noah Claypole, and you work for me. Take down the shutters, you idle young ruffian."

Noah watched as Oliver struggled to remove the heavy shutters from the windows and stow them beside the house, where they were kept during the day. When Oliver finished, he followed Noah down to the kitchen for breakfast.
"Come sit near the fire, Noah," said Charlotte. "I saved you a nice piece of bacon from Master's breakfast."
Then she told Oliver to take some stale bread and sit in the coldest corner of the kitchen. "Hurry up because Master will want you to mind the shop."
"Do you hear, Workhouse?" said Noah. "Hurry up."
"Oh, leave him alone," said Charlotte.
But Noah didn't want to leave Oliver alone. He finally had someone who ranked below him. However, the undertaker soon realized that Oliver was someone special.
"Young Twist is a good-looking boy," said Mr. Sowerberry to his wife one night at supper.
"He should be," replied Mrs. Sowerberry. "He eats enough."
"There's an expression of melancholy in his face, which is very interesting, my dear. He'd make a delightful mourner at funerals."
Mrs. Sowerberry looked at him quizzically.
"I don't mean a regular mourner at adult funerals," continued Mr. Sowerberry. "I'd use him only at children's funerals. It would be delightful to see a small mourner walking with a small coffin."

Oliver soon had a chance to acquire a great deal of experience as a mourner. Thanks to an outbreak of measles, he led many processions to the graveyard. After a month he was formally apprenticed to the undertaker.

Noah was jealous of Oliver's promotion to mourner and so continued to harass him. One day while they were eating, Noah was determined to make Oliver cry. The older boy pulled Oliver's hair and pinched his ears.
"Workhouse, how's your mother?" said Noah.
"She's dead," replied Oliver. "Don't you say anything about her!"
"What did she die of, Workhouse?"
"Of a broken heart. That's what I was told." A tear rolled down Oliver's cheek.
"Oh, what's made you cry?"
"Not you ," Oliver replied sharply. "Don't say anything more about her."
"You might as well know, Workhouse, that your mother was a bad one. If she hadn't died, she'd have ended up in jail."

Crimson with fury, the little boy overturned the table. Oliver grabbed Noah and knocked him to the ground. A minute earlier Oliver had looked like a quiet, dejected creature. But the insult to his mother had set his blood on fire.
"He's trying to murder me!" shouted Noah. "Charlotte! Mrs. Sowerberry! Help me! Oliver's gone mad!"
The two women rushed downstairs into the kitchen.
"You little wretch!" screamed Charlotte, grabbing Oliver by one arm. "Oh, you ungrateful, murderous, horrid villain!" And with every word, she smacked Oliver.

Mrs. Sowerberry and Noah joined in the melee. The three of them managed to drag the struggling boy into the cellar, where they slammed the door and locked it tight. Oliver kicked and kicked the door from the inside.
Mrs. Sowerberry sank into a chair and burst into tears. "Oh, Charlotte! It's a blessing we haven't all been murdered in our beds!"
"He'll kick that door down, and Mr. Sowerberry is away," said Charlotte.
"Noah, run to Mr. Bumble and tell him to come here right now," said Mrs. Sowerberry.
Noah ran to the workhouse gate, where he stopped for a moment to make himself look as pitiful as possible. Then he shouted, "Mr. Bumble! Mr. Bumble!"
The parish officer was so alarmed by these cries that he rushed outside with his hat in his hand.
"What's happened?" Mr. Bumble said breathlessly. "Has Oliver run away?"
"No, sir, but he tried to murder us! Mr. Sowerberry is out, so Mrs. Sowerberry wants you to come and flog Oliver."
Mr. Bumble put on his hat and tapped his cane on the ground. "Let's go."
They hurried to the undertaker's shop, where Oliver was still kicking the cellar door and Mrs. Sowerberry and Charlotte were waiting in fear.
"Oliver!" shouted Mr. Bumble through the keyhole.
"Let me out!"
"Do you know who's speaking to you?"
"Yes."
"Aren't you afraid of me?"
"No!" Oliver replied boldly.
Mr. Bumble staggered back in surprise.
"He must be mad," said Mrs. Sowerberry. "No boy in his right mind would dare speak to you like that."
"It's not madness, ma'am. It's meat. If you had kept the boy on gruel, this never would have happened."
Just then Mr. Sowerberry returned. After hearing what Oliver had done, he dragged the boy from the cellar and beat him.
Mr. Bumble shook his head. "All you can do now is leave him in the cellar for a day or so until he's a little starved. Then take him out and keep him on gruel through his apprenticeship."
So they left Oliver in the cellar for the rest of the day with a slice of bread and some water. That night Mrs. Sowerberry ordered him upstairs to bed.

As he looked around the dismal undertaker's workshop, Oliver fell on his knees and wept. For a long time, he remained motionless, but finally he got up and opened the door. Outside, it was a cold, dark night, and the stars seemed very far away.
Oliver softly closed the door. He tied up his few articles of clothing into a handkerchief. Then he sat on a bench to wait for morning.
When the first ray of daylight struggled through the shutters, Oliver opened the door. He took one last look around the shop. Then he stepped out into the street.
Oliver walked along the main road until he spotted a footpath crossing a field.
"Mr. Bumble brought me on that path when I came to the workhouse," he said to himself. To avoid being noticed, he decided to leave the main road and take the path.

He soon reached Mrs. Mann's farm, where he had lived for the first ten years of his life. No one was stirring at this early hour. Oliver passed by silently and kept on walking. When the path ended, he found himself back on the main road.

The sun was shining brightly now, and Oliver was still afraid someone might see him. So he alternately ran and hid behind bushes. At noon he sat down by a milestone to think about where to go. The milestone said it was seventy miles to London.
"London!" thought Oliver. "Nobody could ever find me in a huge city. Not even Mr. Bumble."

He had often heard the old men in the workhouse say that an enterprising boy would never starve in London. There were ways to earn a living in the city that country people couldn't even imagine. Oliver jumped to his feet and started walking again.
He walked for five more miles before he realized how long it would take him to get to London. Sitting down to rest, he opened his bundle.

"A clean shirt is a very comfortable thing," thought Oliver. "And so are two pairs of darned stockings. A penny and a crust of bread are good too, but they're of little help on a 65-mile walk in wintertime."

Oliver walked twenty miles that day. He ate only the crust of dry bread and drank only a few drinks of water begged from cottages along the road. That night he went into a meadow and slept under a hay wagon. At first he was frightened by the wind moaning dismally over the empty fields. He had never felt so lonely, but exhausted from his journey, he soon fell asleep.

The next morning he was so hungry that he had to use his penny to buy a small loaf of bread. He had walked no more than 12 miles when night closed in again. His feet were sore and his legs were weak. He spent another night outdoors.

The days passed and Oliver kept walking. In some villages he saw large signs warning that beggars would be sent to jail, so he hurried through those villages. In other places he hung around the inns, hoping someone would give him something to eat. He begged at farmhouses, but usually the farmers threatened to set the dogs on him. Oliver would have starved to death without the bread and cheese given to him by a kindhearted toll collector and an old lady.
On the seventh morning after he had run away, he slowly limped into a little town. The sun was rising as Oliver, with bleeding feet and dust-covered clothes, sat on a doorstep.
A boy passed by. He returned a few minutes later and stood across the road, staring at Oliver. Noticing that Oliver was looking at him, the boy crossed the road.
"Hello, my friend," said the boy. "What brings you here?"
Oliver couldn't answer for a moment because he was busy staring at the boy, who was the strangest person he'd ever seen.

He was definitely a boy, but he swaggered like a man. A hat perched precariously on top of his head, and he wore a man's coat that nearly reached his heels. The sleeves were so long that he had to roll them up to see his hands.
"I'm hungry and tired," Oliver finally replied with tears in his eyes. "I've been walking for seven days."
"Seven days!" exclaimed the boy. "That's a long time. If you want food, you shall have it!"

Helping Oliver to stand up, the boy took him to a nearby shop. There he purchased a ham and a loaf of bread. Then he led Oliver to a pub, where he bought something to drink and urged Oliver to eat the bread and ham.
"Going to London?" asked the strange boy when Oliver had finished eating.
"Yes," answered Oliver.
"Got any lodgings?"
"No."
"Got any money?"
"No."
The boy whistled and shook his head.
"Do you live in London?" asked Oliver.
"Yes, I do. I suppose you'll be wanting someplace to sleep tonight."
"Oh, yes," replied Oliver. "I haven't slept under a roof since I left the country."
"Well, don't fret about that. I have to be in London tonight. I know a respectable old gentleman who'll give you lodgings for free."

This unexpected offer was too tempting for Oliver to pass up. He and the boy continued to talk, and Oliver discovered that his name was Jack Dawkins. "But my friends call me the Artful Dodger," said the boy.

For some reason the Dodger didn't want to arrive in London before nightfall. So it was nearly eleven o'clock when they entered the great city. Oliver followed closely behind as his new friend led him into one of the worst parts of the city. Oliver had never seen a dirtier or more wretched place. The streets were narrow and muddy, and the air smelled of filth. At last the Dodger pushed open the door to an old house and whistled loudly.
"Now then!" a strange voice said in reply.
The Dodger uttered a mysterious password and then led Oliver upstairs to a dark and dirty room. Four boys sat at a table watching an old man cook sausages over the fire.
The boys gathered around as the Dodger whispered to the man. Suddenly the Dodger said, "Fagin, this is my friend Oliver Twist," and everyone turned to look.

Now Oliver could see that the man's matted red hair covered much of an ugly face. "Pleased to meet you," he said, taking Oliver's hand and bowing low. The boys crowded around Oliver, shaking his hands and putting their hands into his pockets.
Fagin watched as Oliver stared at the many silk handkerchiefs hanging about the room.
"I see you've noticed our handkerchiefs," said Fagin. "We're just getting them ready for the wash."

The boys all burst into laughter. Oliver was puzzled, but he didn't say anything because the sausages were done and it was time to eat. After supper Oliver settled down on an old sack and went right to sleep on the floor. He could wait until tomorrow to begin his new life in this strange place.

It was late morning when Oliver awoke from a long, sound sleep. There was no one else in the room except Fagin, who was boiling some coffee in a pot for breakfast. The old man was whistling to himself as he stirred the coffee round and round with an iron spoon.

Fagin stopped to listen whenever he heard the smallest sound downstairs. But once he was satisfied no one was there, he went back to stirring and whistling. Oliver watched Fagin through half-closed eyes as he drifted in and out of sleep.
When the coffee was done, Fagin turned around.
"Oliver!" he called softly.

Oliver didn't respond, pretending to be asleep. Fagin stepped gently to the door and latched it. Then he pulled a small box from a trapdoor in the floor. Dragging an old chair to the table, he sat down and opened the box.

Oliver's eyes widened as Fagin pulled out a magnificent gold watch, sparkling with jewels. The old man grinned and muttered some words that Oliver couldn't hear. Out of the box came a dozen more watches, plus rings, necklaces, and bracelets.
Suddenly Fagin looked up, and his eyes met Oliver's. Fagin closed the lid of the box with a loud crash. Trembling with anger, he approached Oliver.
"Why are you watching me? Why are you awake? What have you seen?" cried Fagin. "Speak, boy!"
"I couldn't sleep any longer, sir," Oliver said meekly. "I'm very sorry if I disturbed you, sir."
"Did you see any of these pretty things, my dear?" Fagin laid his hand on the box.
"Yes, sir."
"Ah!" Fagin turned pale. "They . . . they're mine, Oliver. My little property. All I have to live on in my old age. People call me a miser, my dear. I'm just a miser, that's all."
Oliver thought the old gentleman must be a miser. Why else would he live in such a dirty place when he had all those riches? But maybe he was spending all his money caring for the boys.
"May I get up?" asked Oliver.
"Certainly, my dear, certainly. There's a pitcher of water by the door. Bring it here and I'll give you a basin to wash in."

After Oliver washed himself, Fagin told him to empty the basin out the window. Oliver had just finished doing that when the Dodger returned with one of the boys, Charley Bates. They all sat down to breakfast. The Dodger had brought home some rolls and ham in the crown of his hat.
Fagin glanced slyly at Oliver as he spoke to the boys. "Have you been hard at work this morning, my dears?"
"Oh yes," said Charley.
"Good boys! What have you got, Dodger?"
"A couple of wallets." The Dodger handed two wallets to Fagin.
Fagin opened the wallets and inspected the insides. "Nicely lined, but not as heavy as they might be. But very neat and nicely made. The Dodger is an ingenious workman, isn't he, Oliver?"
"Indeed, sir," replied Oliver.
Charley laughed uproariously at this remark to the amazement of Oliver, who didn't see anything to laugh at.
"And what have you got, my dear?" Fagin asked Charley.
"Handkerchiefs." Charley pulled four silk squares from his pockets.

Fagin looked them over carefully. "Well, they're very good. But you haven't monogrammed them nicely at all. All the embroidered initials will have to be picked out with a needle. We'll teach Oliver how to do that. You'd like to make handkerchiefs as easily as Charley, wouldn't you?"
"Very much indeed. If you'll teach me, sir," replied Oliver.
Charley laughed so hard that he almost choked on his coffee. "He's so innocent," Charley said when he could speak again.
Oliver didn't realize that he'd fallen in with a gang of pickpockets. Sometimes the boys stole wallets. And sometimes they took handkerchiefs, which were later resold in shops.
When breakfast was cleared away, Fagin and the two boys played a game that seemed very strange to Oliver.

First Fagin placed a snuffbox in one pocket of his trousers and a wallet in another. He put a watch in his waistcoat pocket and a mock diamond pin in his shirt. He buttoned his coat and put his eyeglass case and his handkerchief in his coat pockets.

Then he trotted back and forth with a walking stick, imitating the way that old gentlemen walked about the city every day. Sometimes he stopped, pretending to study a shop window. He patted his pockets and looked around in such a funny way that Oliver laughed until he cried. At last the Dodger stepped on Fagin's toes while Charley stumbled into him and reached into his pockets.
If Fagin felt a hand in any pocket, he cried out and the game began again. But the game was soon interrupted by the arrival of a young lady named Nancy.
"Pleased to meet you, Oliver," said Nancy.
Oliver thought she seemed very nice, almost like an older sister to the boys. Fagin gave her something to eat, and after chatting awhile, she left with Charley and the Dodger.
"This is a pleasant life, isn't it?" Fagin said to Oliver. "They've gone out for the day."
"Are they going to do some more work?"

"Yes, if there's work to do, they'll find it. Make them your models, my dear." Fagin tapped the fire shovel on the hearth to add emphasis to his words. "Do everything they say and take all their advice, especially the Dodger's. He'll be a great man and he'll make you one, too, if you model yourself after him."
Fagin stared off into the fire. "Is my handkerchief hanging out of my pocket, my dear?"
"Yes, sir."
"See if you can take it out without my feeling anything. Remember how you saw them do that when they were playing earlier."
Oliver held up the bottom of Fagin’s pocket with one hand as he had seen the Dodger hold it. Then with the other hand, he pulled out the handkerchief.
"Is it gone?" cried Fagin.
"Here it is, sir." Oliver showed him the handkerchief.
"I never saw a sharper lad! Here's a shilling for you. If you go on this way, you'll be the greatest man of all. Now come here and I'll show you how to take the monograms out of handkerchiefs."
Oliver didn't understand what this had to do with being a great man. But assuming that the older man knew more than he did, Oliver followed him to the table and was soon engrossed in his new work.

For many days Oliver remained indoors with Fagin. The other boys brought home a great number of handkerchiefs, so he was kept busy picking out the monograms. Every morning Charley and the Dodger played their game with Fagin. Sometimes Oliver joined in, trying to take an item from Fagin before he felt a hand in his pocket.

Oliver began to long for fresh air. He begged Fagin to allow him to go out to work with the others. But Fagin said he wasn't ready yet. Whenever the boys came home empty-handed, Fagin lectured them on the misery of idleness and lazy habits. Then he reinforced the importance of hard work by sending them to bed without supper. Seeing this, Oliver was even more anxious to be actively employed.
For several days there were no handkerchiefs to work on. Then suddenly one morning, Fagin gave Oliver permission to go out.
"I think today would be a good day for you to begin working, my dear," said Fagin.
"Will I be making wallets or handkerchiefs?" Oliver asked innocently.
Charley had another coughing fit over his coffee while the Dodger merely smiled.
"Just follow Charley and the Dodger, and do whatever the Dodger tells you," said Fagin. "Remember, use him as your model."
And so they went out. Oliver walked between the Dodger and Charley. They walked so slowly that Oliver soon began to think his companions were planning to deceive Fagin by not going to work at all.

As they walked along, the Dodger pulled caps from the heads of small boys and tossed them out of reach. Charley took apples and onions from the market stalls and stuffed them into his surprisingly large pockets. This behavior looked very bad to Oliver. He was about to announce that he'd find his own way back to Fagin's when suddenly the Dodger stopped. He put his finger on his lip to silence the others.
"What's the matter?" demanded Oliver.
"Hush!" said the Dodger. "Do you see that old man outside the bookseller's?"
"The old gentleman over there?" said Oliver. "Yes, I see him."
"He'll do," said the Dodger.
"A prime one," observed Charley.

Oliver looked from one to the other with surprise, but he didn't dare ask any questions. Charley and the Dodger walked stealthily across the road and slunk close behind the old gentleman. Oliver walked a few paces after them and, not knowing what to do, looked on in silent amazement.

The old gentleman was a very respectable-looking person with gold spectacles and an elegant bamboo cane. He had picked up a book from a table outside the bookseller's and there he stood, reading away as if he were sitting at home. He didn't appear to notice the street or the boys. Instead he stared only at the book, which he seemed to be reading with the greatest interest and eagerness.

Suddenly, to Oliver's horror, the Dodger plunged his hand into the old man's pocket and pulled out a handkerchief. The Dodger handed it to Charley, and the two of them ran around the corner at full speed.

In that instant Oliver understood the whole mystery of the handkerchiefs, the watches, the jewelry, and the "work" that the boys did for Fagin. He stood for a moment with the blood tingling through his veins from terror. He felt as if he were on fire. Then, confused and frightened, he ran away as fast as he could.

This all happened in an instant. At the very moment when Oliver began to run, the old gentleman put his hand into his pocket. He discovered his handkerchief was missing and turned around. Seeing Oliver running away, he naturally concluded that Oliver was the thief.
"Stop, thief!" shouted the old gentleman as he took off after Oliver with the book still in his hand.

The old gentleman was not the only one who cried out. Charley and the Dodger had not wanted to attract attention by running down the open street. They had merely hidden in the first doorway around the corner. As soon as they saw Oliver running and heard the old gentleman shouting, they knew what had happened.
"Stop, thief!" they shouted as they joined in the pursuit.
This upset Oliver even more. So away he went like the wind with the old gentleman and the two boys roaring and shouting behind him.

Hearing the commotion, the baker threw down his basket. The milkman left his pail. The errand boy abandoned his parcels. The tradesman left his counter. Away they all ran after Oliver, with everyone shouting.
"Stop, thief! Stop, thief!" The cry was taken up by what seemed like a hundred voices.
At last a man caught up to Oliver and dragged him to the ground.
"Give the boy some air!" cried the baker.
"Nonsense! He doesn't deserve it!" said the milkman.
"Here comes the old man!" said the errand boy.
"Is this the boy, sir?" asked the tradesman.
Covered with mud and bleeding from his lip, Oliver lay on the ground. He looked wildly at the faces surrounding him while the old gentleman was dragged into the circle.
"Yes," said the old gentleman, looking Oliver in the eye. "I am afraid it is the boy."
"Afraid!" murmured the crowd. "That's a good one!"
"Poor fellow, he has hurt himself," said the old gentleman.
"I did that, sir, and I cut my knuckle against his teeth," said a burly fellow. "I stopped him, sir."

He touched his hat with a grin, expecting some reward for his pains. But the old gentleman eyed him with an expression of dislike. The old gentleman looked as if he wanted to run away too. But at that moment a police officer made his way through the crowd and seized Oliver by the collar.
"Come on, get up," the policeman said roughly.
"It wasn't me, sir. Indeed it was two other boys," said Oliver, looking around. "They're here somewhere."
"Oh, no, they aren't," said the policeman.
And he was right, because Charley and the Dodger had disappeared down the first alley they'd come to.
"Get up," said the policeman again.
"Don't hurt him," said the old gentleman with concern.
"Oh, I wouldn't think of hurting him," said the policeman sarcastically. "Will you stand upon your legs, you young devil?"

Oliver did not reply, but instead tried to rise to his feet. The policeman grabbed Oliver's jacket collar and dragged him down the street at a rapid pace. The old gentleman walked by the policeman's side, and the crowd followed along behind.

The police station was nearby, so the crowd could only accompany Oliver through two or three streets. But even that short distance seemed to please a tall man wrapped in a dark cloak. As Oliver was led into the court, the man's lips curled in a cruel smile. He disappeared when the crowd broke up.
Oliver was taken to a cell. The old gentleman whose handkerchief had been stolen was instructed to wait in a small room.
"There's something about that boy's face that touches me," the old gentleman said to himself. "Could he be innocent? Where have I seen that face before?"
The old gentleman thought back over the many people he'd known. "No," he said at last. "It must be my imagination."
He picked up the book from the bookshop and started reading again. Soon he was led into the courtroom. Mr. Fang, the magistrate, sat at one end of the room while Oliver sat trembling in a wooden pen.
"Who are you?" Mr. Fang demanded gruffly.
"My name is Brownlow," said the old gentleman.
"And what crime are you charged with?"
"I'm not charged with any crime! My handkerchief was stolen."
"Swear this man in," Mr. Fang instructed a court officer.

And so Mr. Brownlow began to tell his story. He explained that he had chased Oliver because he saw the boy running away. He hoped the magistrate would be lenient if this boy wasn't the thief but merely connected with thieves.
In conclusion Mr. Brownlow said, "The boy has been hurt already." Then looking at Oliver, he said forcefully, "And I fear . . . I really fear that he's ill."
"Oh, yes, I'm sure he's ill," said Mr. Fang with a sneer. He looked at Oliver and said sternly, "I'll have none of your tricks here, you young vagabond. What's your name?"
Oliver tried to reply, but his tongue failed him. The whole room seemed to spin, and he was deadly pale.
"What's your name, you hardened scoundrel?" demanded Mr. Fang. "Officer, what's his name?"

This comment was addressed to a police officer standing next to Oliver. The policeman bent over the boy and repeated the question. But he realized that Oliver couldn't reply. He also knew that this would make the magistrate angry and likely add to the severity of Oliver's punishment.
"He says his name's Tom White, your worship," replied the kindhearted police officer.
"Where does he live?" asked Mr. Fang.
"Wherever he can, your worship," replied the officer, again pretending to hear Oliver's answer.
"Does he have any parents?"
"He says they died in his infancy, your worship," said the officer, making a guess.
At this point Oliver raised his head and looked around with imploring eyes. "Please, may I have a drink of water?" he asked feebly.
"Stuff and nonsense!" said Mr. Fang. "Don't try to make a fool of me."
"I think he really is ill, Your Worship," said the officer.
"I know better," said Mr. Fang.
Mr. Brownlow had been watching Oliver with concern. "Take care of him, Officer. He'll fall down."
"Step back, Officer," said Mr. Fang. "Let him fall if he likes."
And with that, Oliver fainted and fell to the floor. The men in the room looked at each other, but no one dared to move without Mr. Fang's permission.
"I knew he was pretending," Mr. Fang said in a self-satisfied way. "Let him lie there. He'll soon grow tired of his game and get up."
"How do you propose to deal with the case, sir?" asked the clerk in a low voice.
"He is committed to prison for three months," said Mr. Fang. "And sentenced to hard labor, of course. Everyone, clear the courtroom."
The door was opened and a couple of men prepared to carry the unconscious boy to his cell. Suddenly an old man rushed into the courtroom and advanced toward the magistrate.
"Stop, stop! Don't take him away!" The new arrival was breathless with hurry.
"What is this? Who is this? Turn this man out. Clear the courtroom!" cried Mr. Fang.
"I will speak," declared the man. "I will not be turned away. I saw everything. I own the bookshop. I demand that you hear my evidence, Mr. Fang. You must not refuse me."
The man stood in front of the bench, breathing heavily.
"Swear him in," growled Mr. Fang. "Now, man, what have you got to say?"

"This gentleman was reading outside my shop." The man indicated Mr. Brownlow. "I saw three boys—two others and the prisoner here—loitering across the way. The robbery was committed by another boy. I saw it, and I also saw that this boy was perfectly amazed and stupefied by it."
The bookshop owner took a deep breath and then proceeded to relate the exact circumstances of the robbery.
Mr. Fang was clearly annoyed. "Why didn't you come here before?"
"I didn't have anyone to mind the shop," replied the man. "Everybody who could have helped me had joined in the chase. I couldn't get anybody until five minutes ago, and I've run all the way here."
"This man was reading, was he?" Mr. Fang pointed to Mr. Brownlow.
"Yes, the very book he has in his hand."
"Oh, that book. Is it paid for?"
"No, it is not," said the bookseller with a smile.
"Dear me, I forgot all about that!" exclaimed Mr. Brownlow.

"Well, you're a nice person to bring charges against a poor boy!" said Mr. Fang. "You obtained that book under very suspicious and disreputable circumstances. You're lucky that the owner of that book has decided not to prosecute you. Let this be a lesson to you."
"What! But I meant to pay!" exclaimed Mr. Brownlow.
"The boy is discharged. Clear the courtroom!" said Mr. Fang. "Officers, do you hear? Clear the courtroom."

An indignant Mr. Brownlow was escorted from the magistrate's court with the book in one hand and his bamboo cane in the other. But when he reached the pavement, his rage evaporated. Little Oliver Twist lay on the ground with his shirt unbuttoned and his face a deadly white.
"Poor boy, poor boy!" said Mr. Brownlow, bending over him. "Call a coach, somebody."
A coach arrived and Oliver was carefully laid on one seat. Mr. Brownlow got in and sat on the other one.
"May I accompany you?" said the bookseller, looking in.
"Bless me, yes, my dear sir," said Mr. Brownlow. "I still have this unhappy book. Jump in. Poor fellow! There's no time to lose."
The bookseller got into the coach, and away they drove toward Mr. Brownlow's home.

At Mr. Brownlow's home, Oliver was immediately put to bed. Mr. Brownlow's housekeeper sat by the bed, patiently waiting for Oliver to recover from his fever. But for many days, he remained insensible to the goodness of his new friends.
At last he awoke from what seemed to be a long, troubled dream. Feebly raising his head, he said, "Where am I?"
"Hush, my dear," said Mrs. Bedwin, the old housekeeper. "You must be quiet or you'll be ill again. Lie down."
With that, she gently smoothed his hair back from his face. She looked so kind that he put his hand in hers.
"What a grateful little dear," said Mrs. Bedwin with tears in her eyes. "What would his mother think if she could see him now?"
"Perhaps she does see me," whispered Oliver. "I feel as if she's been here with me."
"That was the fever, dear."
"I suppose it was," said Oliver after a moment's silence. "If she'd seen me ill, it would have made her sad. Her face always looks so happy when I dream of her."
Mrs. Bedwin brought Oliver something cool to drink and he fell asleep again.

It was another three days before the fever passed and Oliver was able to sit up. He was still too weak to walk, so Mrs. Bedwin had him carried downstairs to her own little room. Propped up with pillows, he sat in a chair next to the fire while Mrs. Bedwin warmed some broth for him.
"Are you fond of pictures?" asked Mrs. Bedwin, who noticed him studying a portrait on the wall.
"I don't quite know, ma'am. I've seen so few of them. What a beautiful face that lady has. Who is she?"
"I have no idea, my dear."
Mrs. Bedwin handed Oliver a bowl of broth. To him it seemed rich enough to feed a room full of paupers. He continued to stare at the portrait while he sipped his broth.
"It looks as if she wants to speak to me," he said.

Oliver had scarcely swallowed his last bit of broth when there was a knock at the door, and in walked Mr. Brownlow. Oliver tried to stand up as a mark of respect for his benefactor. But he was too weak and sank back into his chair.
"Poor boy!" said Mr. Brownlow. "How do you feel, my dear?"
"Very happy, sir. And very grateful indeed for your goodness toward me."
"I'm glad to hear that, Tom White."
"My name is Oliver Twist, sir."
Mr. Brownlow looked puzzled. "But why did you tell the magistrate your name was Tom White?"
"I didn't, sir."
Mr. Brownlow studied Oliver's face to see if he was lying. And once again he felt strongly that there was something familiar about Oliver.
"You're not angry with me, sir?" asked Oliver.
"No, no . . ." said Mr. Brownlow distractedly. "Look, Mrs. Bedwin, look there!"

He pointed at the portrait and then to Oliver. There was no missing the resemblance between the lady and the boy. Oliver suddenly felt weak, and as the two adults stared at him, he lost consciousness.
Meanwhile, as soon as Oliver had been captured by the police, Charley Bates and the Artful Dodger ran for home.
"Where's Oliver?" thundered Fagin when they arrived.
The two boys looked at each other but said nothing. Fagin grabbed the Dodger by the collar of his huge coat and began shaking him.
"The police have him. That's all there is to the story," said the Dodger. "Let go of me."
And with one jerk, he swung himself out of the coat, which he left in Fagin's hand. He snatched up a toasting fork and poked it at the old man's waistcoat.
"Hey!" cried a new voice. "What's going on here?"
A stoutly built fellow entered the room, accompanied by a shaggy white dog.

"What are you up to, Fagin? Maltreating the boys, you covetous old crook? It's a wonder the boys don't murder you. That's what I'd have done if I were your apprentice, helping you fence stolen goods."
"Hush, Mr. Sikes," said Fagin. "Don't speak so loudly."
"You always mean mischief when you call me Mister Sikes."
"Well then, Bill Sikes," said Fagin, anxious to please. "Would you like a drink?"
"Make sure you don't poison it."
Sikes said this in jest, but Fagin gave an evil leer as he poured out the drink.
After swallowing two or three drinks, Sikes looked at the boys again. This led to a conversation about Oliver.
"I'm afraid he'll say something that'll get us into trouble," said Fagin. "And things might come out even worse for you since you're in the business of robbing houses."
"We have to find out what happened at the police station," said Sikes. "You have to get hold of this boy somehow."
Fagin nodded in agreement, but no one in the room wanted to go anywhere near the police station. Fortunately for them, Nancy arrived just then.
"Nancy will go to the police station, won't you, my dear?" said Fagin.
"She'll go," said Sikes.
"No, she won't, Fagin," said Nancy.
"Yes, she will, Fagin," said Sikes.
And Sikes was right. By alternately threatening and bribing her, the men forced Nancy to go.
"Wait a minute, my dear," said Fagin as Nancy was preparing to leave. He tied a white apron around her waist and gave her a covered basket. "Carry that in one hand; it looks more respectable."
"Oh, my poor little brother!" Nancy exclaimed as she burst into tears. "What has become of him?"
Nancy winked at the men and disappeared out the door.
"Ah, she's a clever one," said Fagin.
Nancy arrived at the police station and went from one cell door to another. But Oliver wasn't in any of the cells, so she was forced to talk to a police officer.
"Have you seen my brother?" she asked. "He's a sweet-faced little dear."
"The gentleman took him," explained the policeman.
Nancy obtained a few more details about Oliver's release and then ran back to Fagin's.
"We must find him!" said Fagin. "Charley! Nancy! Dodger! Do nothing but skulk about until you find him. I'll shut up this place tonight. You'll know where to find me."

With that, he pushed them out the door. Then he barred the door and pulled from its hiding place the box that Oliver had seen. He quickly hid the watches and jewelry underneath his clothing and went out into the city.
When Oliver came down to the housekeeper's room one morning, he glanced up at the portrait of the lady. But it wasn't there anymore.
"Why have they taken it away?" he asked Mrs. Bedwin.
"Mr. Brownlow thought it bothered you. He didn't want it to prevent you from getting well."
"Oh, no, it didn't bother me. I liked to see it. I quite loved it."
"Well, you get better as fast as you can, dear, and it will be hung up again. Now let's talk of something else."

Those were happy days for Oliver. Everything was so quiet and neat in this house. Everybody was so kind and gentle. Mr. Brownlow bought Oliver a new set of clothes and shoes. Oliver gave his old things to a servant who had been nice to him. He wanted her to sell the clothes and keep the money for herself.
Late one afternoon Mr. Brownlow asked Oliver to come upstairs to his study. Oliver found himself in a little room full of books overlooking a pleasant garden. Mr. Brownlow was reading at a table.
"Now I want you to pay attention to what I'm saying," began Mr. Brownlow.
Oliver instantly felt alarmed. "Oh, don't tell me you're going to send me away!"
"My dear child, I will never abandon you unless you give me cause."
"I never will, sir."

"I hope not. I've been deceived in the past by people whom I've tried to help. But I feel strongly that I can trust you. I only want you to know that I've suffered great pain and sorrow so that you'll be careful not to wound me. Now I want to hear your story. Who were your parents? Where did you live?"
But before Oliver could respond, Mrs. Bedwin came in and laid some books on the table. The bookseller's boy had just delivered them.
"Ask the boy to wait," said Mr. Brownlow.
"He has gone, sir," replied Mrs. Bedwin.
"Call down the street after him. The bookseller is a poor man, and these books are not paid for. I want him to have the money today. There are some books to be taken back too."

Mrs. Bedwin and Oliver rushed downstairs. The housekeeper stood on the front step and called for the boy. Oliver ran one way down the street and a servant girl ran the other. Soon Oliver and the girl returned to report that they couldn't find the boy.
"Dear me, I'm very sorry about that," said Mr. Brownlow, who had joined them. "I particularly wished those books to be returned tonight."
"Send Oliver to the bookseller's with them," suggested Mrs. Bedwin.
"Yes, do let me take them, sir," said Oliver. "I'll run all the way."
The old gentleman nodded. "The books are on a chair by my table. Please fetch them."
Delighted to be of use, Oliver brought down the books in a great bustle. He waited, cap in hand, to hear what message he was to take.

"You're to say that you've brought those books back because I've decided not to buy them. You should then pay the four pounds I owe." Mr. Brownlow handed Oliver some money. "This is a five-pound note, so you must bring back the change."
"I'll be back in ten minutes, sir." Oliver put the money in his pocket and picked up the books. Then he made a respectful bow and left the room.
Mrs. Bedwin followed him to the front door. "Bless his sweet face!" she said as Oliver departed. "Somehow I can't bear to let him out of my sight."
At that moment Oliver looked back at her and nodded before he turned the corner. Mrs. Bedwin smiled back at him and closed the door.

Mr. Brownlow had returned to his study upstairs. "Let me see, he'll be back in twenty minutes at the most," he murmured, pulling out his watch and laying it on the table. "It'll be dark by that time."

Meanwhile Oliver walked toward the bookseller's. When he was almost there, he accidentally turned down a side street. He didn't realize his mistake until he was halfway down the street. Thinking it must lead in the right direction, he didn't turn back. He was walking along, thinking how happy he was, when he was startled by a young woman.
"Oh, my dear brother!" she screamed, throwing her arms tightly around his neck.
"Don't!" cried Oliver, struggling. "Let go of me. Who are you? Why are you stopping me?"
The only reply to this was more cries from the young woman, who was wearing a white apron and carrying a little basket.
"Oh, my gracious!" said the young woman. "I've found him! Oh, Oliver! Oh, you naughty boy to make me suffer such distress on your account."
And with that she burst into such tears that a woman passing by asked if she needed a doctor.
"Oh, no, never mind. I'm better now." The young woman grasped Oliver's hand. "Come home right now, you cruel boy."
"What's the matter, ma'am?" inquired the other woman.
"About a month ago he ran away from his parents, who are hardworking and respectable people. He went and joined a group of thieves and almost broke his mother's heart."
"Do go home, you little brute," said the other woman.
"But I don't know her," said Oliver, greatly alarmed. "I don't have a sister or a mother or father. I'm an orphan and I live with Mr. Brownlow now."
"Oh, hear, how he keeps it up," said the young woman.
"Why, it's Nancy!" exclaimed Oliver, who now saw her face for the first time.
"You see, he does know me!" cried Nancy, appealing to the crowd that had begun to gather. "Make him come home before he kills his dear mother and father and breaks my heart."
"What on earth is this?" said a man, bursting out from a pub with a white dog at his heels. "Young Oliver, come home directly."
"I don't belong to them. I don't know them. Help! Help!" Oliver struggled in the man's powerful grasp.
"Yes, I'll help you, you young rascal," said the man. "Whose books are these? You've been stealing them, haven't you?"
With that, he snatched the books from Oliver's grasp and dragged the boy away.

At Mr. Brownlow's house, the gas lamps were lighted. Mrs. Bedwin was waiting anxiously at the open door. A servant had run up the street many times to see if there was any trace of Oliver. And Mr. Brownlow sat in his dark study with his watch on the table.
Bill Sikes dragged Oliver through the narrow streets so quickly that Nancy had trouble keeping up.
"Grab hold of her hand," Sikes said roughly to Oliver. "And don't you dare make a sound."
They were in a dark corner, out of view of any passersby. Oliver realized there was no point in resisting. He held out his hand, which Nancy clasped tightly.
"Give me the other hand," said Sikes. "Here, Bull's-eye!" he called to the white dog.
The dog looked up and growled.
"See here, dog. If this boy cries out, grab him and hold on tight. Do you understand?"
The dog looked menacingly at Oliver and growled again.
They set off again into the dark night. The lights in the shops were dim through the heavy mist. Bill was dragging Oliver past the prison when a church bell struck the hour.
"I wonder whether the prisoners can hear that," said Nancy.
"Of course they can," replied Sikes. "The last time I was locked up for housebreaking, I could hear every sound at night."
"Poor fellows," said Nancy, who was still looking at the prison.

But there wasn't time to think about prisoners. Sikes yanked on Oliver's wrist, and Nancy came along too. They walked through deserted streets for half an hour. At last they stopped in front of a run-down house with an ancient "For Rent" sign on the door.

Nancy rang the bell. Then they crossed the street and stood under a streetlamp so someone inside could see who they were. At last the door softly opened. Sikes seized a terrified Oliver by the collar, and they went quickly inside the house.
The hallway was very dark. They waited while the person who had let them in barred the door. Then he lit a candle. It was the Artful Dodger. He grinned at Oliver but didn't say anything.
He led them downstairs and through an empty kitchen. When he opened the door to a low room, they were greeted with shouts of laughter from Charley Bates.
"Oh, my goodness!" cried Charley. "Here he is! Look at him, Fagin! Hold me, somebody, or I'll die laughing."
At this, Charley fell on the floor and rolled around and laughed some more. Then he jumped up and held the candle so close to Oliver's new jacket that it nearly caught fire.
"Look at his clothes, Fagin! Superfine cloth and a stylish cut! And his books too. He's such a gentleman now."
"Delighted to see you looking so well," Fagin said to Oliver with mock humility. "Why didn't you write, my dear, and say you were coming? We'd have warmed something up for supper."
Oliver was too shaken to respond. He didn't even react when the Dodger started going through his pockets.
"What's this?" cried the Dodger, holding up the five-pound note that Mr. Brownlow had given Oliver.
"That's mine, Fagin," said Sikes as Fagin seized the note.
"No, it's mine," said Fagin. "You shall have the books, Bill."
"Hand it over," said Sikes. "Do you think Nancy and I have nothing to do but kidnap every boy that escapes from you? If you don't give me that money, I'll take the boy back again."
Fagin started in surprise. Oliver started too, but for a different reason. He hoped that their dispute might really result in his being taken back to Mr. Brownlow.
Sikes plucked the note from Fagin's hand. Looking the old man coolly in the face, Sikes folded up the note and tied it in his neckerchief.
"That's for our share of the trouble," he said. "Keep the books and sell them if you're not fond of reading."
"They're very pretty," said Charley, pretending to read one. "Beautiful writing, isn't it, Oliver?"

"They belong to the kind gentleman who took care of me," said Oliver in distress. "I would have died from the fever if it weren't for him and the housekeeper. Oh, please send back the books and the money. The gentleman will think I stole them."
With these pleading words, Oliver fell on his knees in front of Fagin.
"You're right, Oliver." Fagin looked around at the others in the room. "This couldn't have happened better if we'd planned it."
"But they won't go looking for him," said Sikes. "They're soft-hearted people. They know if he's found, they'll have to bring charges and he'll get sent to prison."
Oliver looked from one person to the other. Suddenly he jumped to his feet and tore wildly from the room, uttering shrieks for help that made the old house echo.
"Don't let the dog go after him, Bill." Nancy sprang to the door and closed it as Fagin, the Dodger, and Charley ran after Oliver. "The dog will tear him to pieces."
"That would serve him right." Sikes grabbed Nancy's wrists and they began to struggle.
"What's the matter here?" cried Fagin as he and the boys returned with Oliver.
"The girl's gone mad," said Sikes.
"No, she hasn't," retorted Nancy.
Fagin turned his attention to Oliver. "So you wanted to get away from me, my dear? Wanted to call the police for assistance?" He picked up a club lying near the fireplace. "We'll cure you of that."
Nancy rushed forward and flung the club into the fire.
"I won't stand by and let you hurt him," she shouted. "He's a thief, a liar, and all that's bad from this night forward. Isn't that enough?"
"You're a fine one to talk," said Sikes.
"I know I am." Nancy turned her anger on Fagin. "I've thieved for you ever since I was half as old as Oliver. I know what kind of life you're leading him into. You're the wretch who ruined my life."
And with that, she rushed at Fagin. She probably would have pummeled him with her fists if Sikes hadn't grabbed her and held her back. Nancy struggled for a moment and then fainted.
Fagin wiped his forehead and smiled at Oliver. "Charley, show Oliver to bed."
"He shouldn't wear his best clothes tomorrow, should he?" asked Charley.
"Certainly not," Fagin replied.
Charley led Oliver into the kitchen where there were several sacks on the floor for beds. And here Charley produced the old clothes that Oliver had given to Mr. Brownlow's servant.
"Fagin knows everyone who's got clothes for sale," explained Charley. "He came upon yours and knew you'd want them back."
Oliver took off his new clothes and handed them to Charley.
"What fun this is!" said Charley. Then he departed from the room, leaving Oliver in the dark and locking the door behind him.

Meanwhile, back in the town of Oliver's birth, Mr. Bumble was about to set off on a trip to London. He was feeling quite important this morning because the workhouse board had appointed him to take two paupers to the city. He was going to appear before a court to argue that they belonged to another parish.

So Mr. Bumble took his place on top of the coach, accompanied by the two men in their ragged clothes. Throughout the trip the paupers persisted in shivering and complaining about the cold. This annoyed Mr. Bumble and made his teeth chatter even though he was wearing a heavy coat. By evening they reached London.

Having disposed of the paupers in a workhouse for the night, Mr. Bumble settled himself at a warm and cozy inn. He had a modest dinner of steaks, oyster sauce, and fine wine. After dinner he set a drink on the mantel and pulled his chair over to the fire. Then he composed himself for an evening of reading the newspaper.
The very first paragraph on which his eye rested was the following advertisement:
FIVE POUNDS REWARD
A young boy named Oliver Twist ran away, or was enticed away, from his home
last Thursday. He has not been seen or heard from since. The above reward will
be paid to any person who gives information that leads to the discovery of
Oliver Twist. The above reward is also offered to anyone who can throw light
on the boy's previous history. The advertiser has many reasons for being
interested in the boy's past.
Mr. Bumble opened his eyes in surprise. There followed a full description of Oliver's clothing and appearance, with Mr. Brownlow's name and address underneath.
Mr. Bumble read the advertisement slowly and carefully three times. And in something more than five minutes, he was on his way to Mr. Brownlow's house, having left his drink untasted on the mantel.
"Is Mr. Brownlow at home?" inquired Mr. Bumble of the servant girl who opened the door.
The girl replied as any good servant would: "I don't know, sir. What is the nature of your business with him?"

Mr. Bumble explained that he had come in reference to the advertisement about Oliver Twist. Hearing that, Mrs. Bedwin, who had been standing at the parlor door, hurried into the hall in a breathless state.
"Come in, come in," said the old woman. "I knew we would hear of him. Poor dear! I knew we would. I was certain of it. Bless his heart. I said so all along."

Having said this, the housekeeper hurried back into the parlor again. She sat down on the sofa and burst into tears. Meanwhile the girl had run upstairs and now returned with a request that Mr. Bumble follow her immediately.
She showed him upstairs into Mr. Brownlow's study.
"Take a seat, will you?" said Mr. Brownlow. He moved the lamp so as to obtain a good view of Mr. Bumble's face. "Now, sir, you have come as a result of seeing the newspaper advertisement?"
"Yes, sir," said Mr. Bumble as he took a seat.
"Do you know where this poor boy is now?" asked Mr. Brownlow with a look of deep concern on his face.
"No, I don't."
"Then what do you know of him?" Mr. Brownlow said impatiently. "Please tell me what you know about Oliver as quickly as possible."
Mr. Bumble put down his hat, unbuttoned his coat, folded his arms, and bowed his head in a thoughtful manner. After a few moments of reflection, he began his story.

"I am the parish officer at the workhouse where Oliver was born. Young Oliver was an orphan, the son of low and vicious parents. Despite a large reward, we have never been able to determine their names. From the moment of his birth, Oliver displayed no better qualities than treachery, ingratitude, and malice."
Here Mr. Bumble paused to let his words sink in.
Mr. Brownlow said nothing, but he looked very serious. "Go on," he said to the parish officer.

"Oliver was apprenticed to an undertaker, a position that any boy would be happy and grateful for. But was he grateful? No. He viciously attacked a defenseless boy who was also employed there, and he terrorized the undertaker's wife and a female servant. Young Twist knew that he deserved a most horrible punishment. So what do you think he did?"
"I don't know," said Mr. Brownlow, who at this point was feeling that he didn't know Oliver at all.
"He ran away from his master's house. So, you see, he has a history of running away."

"I fear that what you say is true." Mr. Brownlow shook his head sadly. He handed a five-pound note to Mr. Bumble. "This is not much for your information. I would gladly have given you three times as much money if your report had been favorable to the boy."

If only Mr. Bumble had known that! He might have presented his little history with a very different slant. It was too late to do that now, however, so he shook his head gravely and pocketed the money.
After Mr. Bumble left, Mr. Brownlow paced the room for a few minutes. He was very disturbed by the parish officer's tale. At last he stopped and rang the bell violently.
"Mrs. Bedwin," said Mr. Brownlow, when the housekeeper appeared. "That boy Oliver is an impostor."
"It can't be, sir. It cannot be," insisted the housekeeper.
"What do you mean by that?" retorted Mr. Brownlow. "I tell you he is an impostor. I have just heard a full account of him from birth. He has been a thorough villain all his life."
"I never will believe it," Mrs. Bedwin replied indignantly. "He was a dear, grateful, gentle child, sir."

"Silence!" ordered Mr. Brownlow. "Never let me hear the boy's name again. I rang to tell you that. Never, never, on any pretense. You may leave the room, Mrs. Bedwin. Remember, I am in earnest about this."
There were sad hearts at Mr. Brownlow's house that night. Although Mr. Brownlow sounded angry, he was more disappointed than truly angry.

Back at Fagin's house, Oliver's heart sank whenever he thought of his warm, kind friends. It was a good thing that he did not know what they had heard that day. If he had known about Mr. Bumble's words, his heart might have broken completely.
The next day Charley and the Dodger went out to work as usual. Fagin took the opportunity to lecture Oliver on the sin of ingratitude. The old man clearly thought Oliver was guilty of that sin.
"Remember who took you in, my dear," said Fagin. "I cherished you. Without my timely aid, you might have perished from hunger."
Fagin smiled hideously and patted Oliver's head. "But if you behave and apply yourself to business, there's a chance we'll still be very good friends."
Oliver did not want to be friends with Fagin. Taking his hat and wrapping himself in an old, patched coat, Fagin left the room. Oliver heard him lock the door.

And so Oliver remained all that day and for many more days. He saw no one between the early morning hours and midnight. He was alone with his thoughts, and those always turned toward his kind friends—Mr. Brownlow and Mrs. Bedwin. Oliver was miserable indeed.

After about a week, Fagin left the door to the room unlocked, so Oliver was free to wander about the house. Looking at the ornate fireplaces and intricately carved woodwork, Oliver concluded that the house had once belonged to better people. But now it was a dismal and dreary place. Spiders had built their webs in the corners, and mice sometimes scampered across the floor.

The shutters were closed tight over all the windows, so only tiny cracks of light entered the rooms. On the top floor, there was one room with bars over the window instead of shutters. Oliver often gazed out this window for hours at a time. But all he could see were the roofs of other houses and their blackened chimney tops.
One afternoon Charley and the Dodger were making plans. "Oh, Oliver," called the Dodger. "My boots need cleaning before I can go out this evening like a proper gent. Come here and clean them."

Oliver was so lonely that he was glad to make himself useful. The Dodger sat on the kitchen table while Oliver knelt on the floor, holding the Dodger's foot in his lap. Charley stood around and watched.
"Why won't you work for Fagin?" Charley asked as Oliver scraped the mud from the Dodger's left boot.
"You'd make a fortune," said the Dodger, swinging his right leg.
"I don't like it," Oliver said timidly. "I wish he'd let me go. I . . . I'd rather go."
"And Fagin would rather not let you go," said Charley with a laugh.
Oliver knew this was true, but he thought it might be dangerous to express his feelings more openly. So he only sighed and went on with his boot cleaning.
"Come on," said Charley. "You know we're the only friends you've got now."
"Some friends." Oliver stopped working. "You ran off and let me get punished for something you did."
"Had to," said the Dodger. "The police know we work for Fagin. He might have gotten into trouble if we'd been caught."
Oliver didn't say anything as he finished polishing the Dodger's boots.

"You know what your problem is?" said the Dodger as he admired his shiny black boots. "You've not been brought up properly. But Fagin will make something of you. And if you don't steal watches and handkerchiefs, someone else will. So you might as well do it and get the money."
"That's all true," said Fagin, who had entered the room unseen by Oliver. "Now, everyone, come sit by the fire."

The boys pulled some chairs close to the fire, and Fagin insisted that Oliver sit next to him. Fagin was so charming that night and his stories were so amusing that Oliver found himself laughing heartily despite his better judgment.

From that day Oliver was seldom left alone but spent many hours with the two boys. They all took turns playing their old game with Fagin, who also entertained them with stories of robberies he'd committed years ago. For Oliver, anything was better than being left alone with only his own sad thoughts for company. Fagin was slowly winning him over.
One cold, damp night, Fagin left the boys at home while he went out. He had business to discuss with Bill Sikes at his house. Nancy opened the door. Sikes and his dog were sitting by the fire.
"What's happening with the house in Chertsey? When are you and Toby Crackit going to rob it?" asked Fagin once Nancy had brought him a drink.
Sikes shook his head. "Toby's been hanging about the place for two weeks. He can't bribe any of the servants to help us. We might still be able to do it, but we'd need a small boy."
"Oh, so you're going to slip him through a window?" asked Fagin.
"Never you mind what we're going to do. Just get me a boy."
"Oliver is a small boy," said Nancy.
"That he is," said Fagin, "and it's time he started working for his bread. He'll do anything you want as long as you frighten him enough."
"Oh, I'll frighten him," said Sikes. "You don't need to worry about that."
"Good!" said Fagin enthusiastically. "Once we fill his mind with the idea that he has been a thief, he's ours. He'll be ours for life!" Fagin crossed his arms and hugged himself with joy.
"Ours!" said Sikes. "Yours, you mean."
"Perhaps I do."
"And what makes you take such pains with one pale kid when there are fifty boys on the streets of London that you might choose from?"

"Because they're of no use to me. Their looks convict them when they get into trouble. But this boy appears so innocent. If I properly manage him . . ." Fagin gazed into the fire. "Never mind why I want him. Now when are you going to rob this house in Chertsey?"

After some discussion it was agreed that Nancy would go to Fagin's the next night and bring Oliver back to Sikes. Oliver would trust her because she had protected him when Fagin wanted to beat him. The following day they would set out for Chertsey. With their arrangements settled, Fagin went out into the night. When he reached his gloomy home, the Dodger answered the door.
"Is Oliver in bed? I want to speak to him," said Fagin as they went into the kitchen.
"Here he is," said the Dodger softly.
Oliver was lying fast asleep on the floor. His face was pale with anxiety and sadness.
"Not now, not yet," murmured Fagin. "I'll wait until tomorrow."

When Oliver awoke the next morning, he was surprised to find a new pair of shoes on the floor next to his bed. He hoped this meant that Fagin was going to release him. But his hope disappeared as soon as he sat down to breakfast.
"You're going to be taken to the residence of Bill Sikes tonight, my dear," said Fagin.
"To . . . to . . . stay there, sir?" Oliver asked anxiously.
"No, no, my dear. We wouldn't like to lose you. Don't be afraid, Oliver. You'll come back to us again. We wouldn't be so cruel as to send you away. Oh no."
The old man was stooping over the fire, toasting a piece of bread. He turned around and looked at Oliver as if he knew that the boy wanted to escape.
"I suppose you want to know why you're going to Bill's." Fagin fixed his eyes on Oliver.
"Yes, sir."
"Why do you think you're going?"
"Indeed I don't know, sir," replied Oliver.
"Bah!" said Fagin, turning back to the fire. "Wait until Bill tells you then."
For the rest of the day, Fagin was in a sour and silent mood. In the evening he prepared to go out.
"You may burn a candle," he said, putting one on the table. "And here's a book for you to read until they come to fetch you. Good night."
"Good night!" Oliver said softly.
Fagin started to leave, but then he turned around. "Take heed, Oliver! Bill Sikes is a dangerous man. Do whatever he tells you to do. And no matter what happens, say nothing."

The old man disappeared. Oliver sat with his head in his hands, pondering with a trembling heart the words he had just heard. At last he picked up the book and began to read. It was a history of the lives and trials of great criminals. And it was so frightening that Oliver slammed the book shut. He heard a rustling sound.
"Who's there?" he cried, catching sight of a figure standing by the door.
"Only me," said a tremulous voice.
Oliver raised the candle and saw Nancy, looking pale and ill.
"Has anything happened?" asked Oliver. "Can I help you? I will if I can."
"God forgive me!" exclaimed the young woman.
"What? Why?"
Nancy struggled to compose herself. "Oh, it's nothing. Are you ready to go with me to Bill?"
"What for?"
Nancy avoided looking Oliver in the eye. "Oh, for no harm."
"I don't believe it."
"Fine, have it your way. For no good then."

Suddenly she stooped over him and whispered, "I saved you from harm once, and I will again. This is not the time to try to escape. If you do, you may be the cause of my death. Now come with me and be quiet."

She held out her hand, and Oliver instinctively took it. A carriage was waiting outside the house, and they quickly climbed into it. Within a few minutes, they were at the house that Fagin had visited the previous evening.
"So you've got the kid," said Sikes when they arrived. "Did he come quietly?"
"Quiet as a lamb," said Nancy.
"Good."
He pulled off Oliver's cap and threw it into a corner. Then taking Oliver by the shoulder, he sat down at the table and stood the boy in front of him.
"If you speak a word when you're out with me . . ."
Sikes went on to threaten Oliver, who winced as he tried not to listen. He didn't need to hear the words to know that his life was in danger.
Oliver didn't have much appetite for supper and went to bed soon after.

The next morning Nancy called him at five o'clock. Rain was beating against the windowpanes. After a quick breakfast, Sikes and Oliver headed out. They were on the road all day, traveling on foot and by wagon for more than 25 miles.
By seven o'clock that night, they stood before a ruined and decayed house. It was dark and appeared uninhabited. But Sikes opened the door and found Toby Crackit sitting by the fire.
"Bill, I'm glad to see you!" said Crackit. "I was afraid you'd given up. But who's this?"
"One of Fagin's boys," said Sikes, pulling a chair toward the fire.
"What an innocent face!" said Crackit. "That'll be invaluable for picking old ladies' pockets at church."
"Enough of that. Give us something to eat and drink. It'll soon be time to go out again."
The men ate heartily, but Oliver could only force down a small crust of bread. Then they all dozed in front of the fire.

Suddenly Toby Crackit declared it was half past one o'clock. In an instant Sikes jumped up and began preparations to go out. Wrapping themselves in large scarves and heavy overcoats, they gathered up an odd assortment of tools.
The two robbers went out the door with Oliver between them. It was now intensely dark. The fog was heavy, and the air was so cold and damp that Oliver's hair and eyebrows froze.
They passed through the town of Chertsey and turned up a road. Soon they came to a house surrounded by a wall. Crackit went over first, and then Sikes gave Oliver a boost.
And now, for the first time, Oliver realized that they were going to rob the house. Filled with terror, he sank to his knees.
"Oh, let me go!" he pleaded. "I'll never come near London, never, never! Have mercy on me and don't make me steal."
"Get up!" muttered Sikes, trembling with rage. "And do what I tell you."

They crept toward the back of the house, where a little window was covered by a shutter. While Crackit used a crowbar to pry off the shutter, Sikes whispered instructions in Oliver's ear. His job was to go through the window, walk along a hallway to the front of the house, and open the door for Sikes and Crackit.
Sikes boosted Oliver up to the window and handed him a lantern. "Here, take this light."
Oliver landed in a small room. Up ahead he could see a flight of stairs. And suddenly he decided to warn the inhabitants, no matter what happened to him. He started to run toward the stairs.
"Wait!" called Sikes. "Come back!"
Startled, Oliver dropped the lantern with a loud clatter.
"Who's that?" called a voice.
A vision of two men at the top of the stairs swam before Oliver's eyes. Then one of them fired a gun, and Oliver fell, wounded.

Three nights later the matron of the workhouse where Oliver was born was having tea. Outside the snow lay frozen in a hard, thick crust and the wind howled sharply. But everything was warm and cozy inside the room belonging to Mrs. Corney. The widow sat at a table in front of the cheerful fire and looked around with a self-satisfied air.
"Well," she said to herself. "We all have much to be grateful for, being indoors on a bitter night like this one."
Mrs. Corney had just tasted her first cup of tea when she was disturbed by a rap on her door.
"Come in," said Mrs. Corney sharply. "Some old woman is probably dying. They always die when I'm at meals. What's wrong?"
"Nothing, ma'am, nothing," said a man's voice.
"Dear me!" the matron exclaimed in a much sweeter tone. "Is that Mr. Bumble?"
"At your service, ma'am." The parish officer was carrying his hat in one hand and a bundle in the other.
"Bad weather, Mr. Bumble."
"Bad indeed, ma'am. This very afternoon we gave away twenty loaves of bread and a cheese and a half, and still those paupers are not content."
"Of course not. When would they be?" said the matron, sipping her tea.
"When indeed." Mr. Bumble unpacked his bundle. "I brought the port wine that the board ordered for the infirmary."
He placed the two bottles on top of a chest of drawers and folded up the handkerchief in which they had been wrapped. He put that in his pocket and picked up his hat as if preparing to go.
"You'll have a very cold walk," said the matron.
"The wind blows sharply tonight, ma'am." Mr. Bumble turned up his coat collar.
"Would you stay and take a cup of tea?" she inquired shyly.
