Mr. Bumble instantly turned down his collar and took a seat before the fire. Mrs. Corney rose to get another cup and saucer. As she sat down, her eyes met Mr. Bumble's, and she blushed.
"Sweet, Mr. Bumble?" she inquired, picking up the sugar.
"Very sweet indeed, ma'am." He regarded her tenderly. As she handed him a cup of tea, he squeezed her little finger.

They talked of Mrs. Corney's cat and kittens. They drank more tea, and Mr. Bumble edged his chair around the table until it touched Mrs. Corney's chair. The parish officer drank his last drop of tea, ate a piece of toast, and kissed the matron.
"Mr. Bumble!" exclaimed Mrs. Corney in a whisper. She was so startled that she had quite lost her voice. "Mr. Bumble, I shall scream!"

Mr. Bumble made no reply but put his arm around her waist. Mrs. Corney would have screamed, except just then there was a hasty knocking at the door. Mr. Bumble darted to the wine bottles and began dusting them with great energy.
"Who's there?" Mrs. Corney demanded in her usual sharp voice.
An old pauper woman put her head in at the door. "If you please, mistress, Old Sally is dying."
"Well, what's that to me?" angrily demanded the matron. "I can't keep her alive, can I?"
"No, mistress. She says she has something to tell you."
With much annoyance, Mrs. Corney wrapped herself in a shawl and followed the woman. Sally was sitting up in bed when they arrived at her bedside.
"You must lie down," said the pauper woman, helping Sally back onto her pillow.
"Send her away," said Old Sally to Mrs. Corney. "Make haste."
Mrs. Corney dismissed the pauper woman. Sally reached out a hand and pulled her down into a chair.
"Now listen to me," said the dying woman. "In this very room I once nursed a pretty young creature. She gave birth to a boy and died. Let me think . . . what was the year?"
"Never mind the year. What about her?"
"She was barely dead when I stole it. The only thing she had. A necklace. Gold. Pure gold. She could have sold it for food or clothing, but she kept it safe around her neck."
"Gold!" Mrs. Corney bent eagerly over the dying woman. "Go on. What happened to it?"
"And the boy . . ."
"What boy?"
"They named him Oliver. He grew to look so like his mother. Poor girl. I always thought of her whenever I saw him."
"But the necklace. What did you do with the necklace?"
Sally pulled the matron closer and whispered something. Then she closed her eyes and died. Mrs. Corney quickly left the room.
"She had nothing to tell me after all," Mrs. Corney said to the pauper woman, who was waiting in the hall.

Meanwhile Mr. Bumble had been left by himself in Mrs. Corney's room. He opened the closet, counted the teaspoons, weighed the sugar tongs in his hand, and inspected a milk pot to be sure it was genuine silver. Trying to decide how much she was worth, he then sat down to take an inventory of the furniture.

Still Mrs. Corney did not return. He recounted the teaspoons and double-checked the condition of the furniture. Perhaps, he thought, he should have a quick glance through the contents of Mrs. Corney's chest of drawers.

Mr. Bumble listened at the keyhole to make sure no one was coming. Then he opened the three long drawers. Among the various garments of good fashion and texture, he found a small padlocked box. Mr. Bumble shook the box and it gave forth a pleasant sound like the clinking of coins.
Mr. Bumble returned with a stately walk to the fireplace. "I'll do it!" he declared to himself.
Just then Mrs. Corney burst into the room in a state of agitation.
"What's wrong?" asked the parish officer in alarm.
"Oh, nothing, nothing," she said breathlessly. "Tea! I must have more tea."
Mr. Bumble bustled about, making another pot of tea. He watched with concern as Mrs. Corney drank the hot liquid. The tea had a settling effect upon her.
"You know the master of the workhouse is dying, my dear?" he said.
"Yes."

"He may not live another week, and his death will open up a vacancy that perhaps I might fill." Mr. Bumble suddenly grasped her hands. "Oh, Mrs. Corney, what a prospect this opens! What an opportunity for a joining of our hearts! Will you say yes to me?"
"Yes!"
And with that the happy couple was engaged to be married. But Mr. Bumble had one more question.
"What was it that agitated you so?"
"Nothing in particular," Mrs. Corney said evasively. "I'll tell you sometime after we're married, dear."

While Mr. Bumble was proposing to Mrs. Corney, Fagin sat brooding in front of his own fire. At a table behind him, the Artful Dodger played cards with Charley Bates. As it was a cold night, the Dodger wore his hat. He and Charley laughed and joked while they played.
"Hark!" the Dodger cried suddenly. "I heard the bell."
Taking the only candle, he crept softly upstairs to open the door.
The bell was rung again with some impatience while Fagin and Charley waited below in darkness. After a short pause, the Dodger reappeared and whispered to Fagin.
"What!" cried Fagin. "He's alone?"
The Dodger nodded to Fagin. He also signaled to Charley that now would not be a good time for joking.
Fagin looked as if he dreaded hearing some terrible news.
"Where is he?" asked Fagin.
The Dodger pointed upstairs.
"Bring him down immediately."

The Dodger went upstairs. He returned, followed by a man wearing a heavy coat. After a hurried glance around the room, the man pulled off a large scarf that had concealed the lower part of his face. It was Toby Crackit.
"How are you, Fagin?" said Toby. "I can't talk business till I've had something to eat and drink. I've had nothing for three days."

Fagin signaled for the Dodger to bring some food and drink. Then he motioned for Toby to sit at the table. Once the meal arrived, Fagin dismissed the boys and took a seat at the table. Toby ate his food slowly, in no hurry to tell his story. Meanwhile Fagin waited in agony.
At last Toby was ready to talk. He wiped his mouth and stretched.
"First and foremost, Fagin, how's Bill?"
"What?" screamed Fagin, jumping up from his seat.
"Why, you don't mean to say . . . ," began Toby, turning pale.
"Where are they?" cried Fagin, stamping his foot furiously on the floor. "Sikes and the boy! Where are they hiding? Why have they not been here?"
"The robbery failed," Toby said faintly.
"Yes, I know that." Fagin tore a newspaper page from his pocket and pointed to it. "What else happened?"
"Someone fired a gun and hit the boy. We ran through the fields carrying him between us. They gave chase through hedge and ditch. The whole village was awake, and the dogs were after us."
"And Oliver?"

"His head hung down and he was cold. They were close on our heels. It was every man for himself to avoid the gallows! Bill and I parted company and left the boy lying in a ditch. Dead or alive, that's all I know about him."
Fagin waited to hear no more. Uttering a yell, he rushed from the room and from the house.
The old man reached the street corner. He was pressing onward in the same wild manner when suddenly a carriage dashed past and forced him out of the street and onto the pavement.

At last he came to a narrow and dismal alley leading to Saffron Hill. In its filthy shops were huge bunches of secondhand silk handkerchiefs. They were of all sizes and patterns. Hundreds of these handkerchiefs dangled from pegs outside the shop windows.

It was into this part of the city that Fagin turned. He was well known to the citizens of this alley, who were all in the business of buying and selling stolen goods. They nodded familiarly to him as he passed, but he didn't stop. Fagin was heading for a certain pub, the one where Bill Sikes and his dog could often be found.

At the pub Fagin made a sign to the man at the bar and walked straight upstairs. He opened the door to a large, dark room that was filled with people. Looking around anxiously, he seemed to be in search of some particular person. He beckoned to the landlord and quietly left the room.
"What can I do for you, Mr. Fagin?" inquired the man as he followed him out to the landing. "Won't you join us?"
Fagin shook his head impatiently and whispered, "Is he here?"
"No."
"And no news of Bill Sikes either?"
"None," replied the landlord. "Bill won't stir until it's safe. Depend on that. The police are on the scent down there, and if he moved, he'd blow the whole thing."
"Will he be here tonight?" Fagin asked again.
"Do you mean Monks?"
"Hush," said Fagin. "Yes."
"I expected him before now. If you'll wait ten minutes, he'll probably . . ."
"No, no," said Fagin hastily. "Tell him I was here and that he must come to see me tomorrow night."
With that, Fagin went downstairs and out into the street. He hailed a carriage and rode to within a half mile of Bill Sikes' house. Then he got out and walked the rest of the way.
He arrived to find no one at Bill Sikes' house but Nancy. She was sleeping with her head upon the table. She looked up as he closed the door.
"Where do you think Bill is now, my dear?" asked Fagin.
"I can't say," muttered Nancy, laying her head back down on the table.
Fagin told her everything he'd learned from Toby Crackit. "And Oliver. Poor little boy. Left in a ditch, Nancy!"
"The boy is better off where he is," said Nancy, suddenly looking up. "And if no harm comes to Bill from it, I hope Oliver lies dead in that ditch."
"What?" cried Fagin in amazement.

"Yes, I do," said Nancy, meeting his gaze. "I shall be glad to have him out of my sight and to know that the worst is over. I can't bear to have him near me. The sight of him turns me against myself and all of you."
"If Sikes comes back and leaves the boy behind, dead or alive . . ." Fagin said angrily.
"What's all this about?" cried Nancy.
"That boy's worth hundreds of pounds to me," raged Fagin. "And I'm bound to someone, a devil that only wants the will and has the power to . . ."
Suddenly he stopped and his whole demeanor changed. He unclenched his fists and sank quietly into a chair as if afraid that he'd revealed too much.
"Nancy, dear," said Fagin in his usual voice.
"Don't bother me now. I want to sleep. If Toby got away, Bill's pretty sure to be safe too."
"And the boy?"
Briefly Nancy raised her head again. "He'll have to take his chances with the rest of them."

It was almost midnight when Fagin left Nancy. As the night was piercing cold, he had no temptation to loiter. A sharp wind scoured the streets and seemed to clear them of people. Fagin trembled and shivered as every fresh gust drove him on his way.
At the corner of his own street, he fumbled in his pocket for his key. A dark figure emerged from the shadow of a doorway and glided up to him.
"Fagin!" whispered a voice close to his ear.
"Ah!" The old man quickly stopped and turned around. "Is that—"
"Yes!" interrupted the stranger. "I have been lingering here for two hours. Where have you been?"
"On your business, my dear." Fagin glanced uneasily at his companion.
"Oh, of course." The stranger sneered. "Well, and what's come of it?"
"Nothing good."
The stranger gave Fagin a startled look. "Nothing bad, I hope?"
Fagin shook his head and started to walk again. When they arrived in front of Fagin's house, the stranger said he wanted to talk inside.
"My blood is chilled from standing about so long," he added. "The wind was blowing right through me."

Fagin did not want to let the man into his house, so he muttered something about not having a fire. But the stranger repeated his request as a demand. At last Fagin unlocked the door, and they both went inside.
"It's as dark as a grave in here," said the man, groping forward a few steps. "Make haste with a light."
"Shut the door," whispered Fagin from the end of the hall. As he spoke, the door closed with a loud noise.
"That wasn't my doing," said the other man, feeling his way slowly forward. "The wind blew it closed, or it shut by itself."

Fagin stealthily descended the stairs to the kitchen. He soon returned with a lighted candle and the news that Toby Crackit and the boys were asleep below. Beckoning the man to follow him, he led the way upstairs to the second floor.

"We can say the few words we've got to say in here, my dear." Fagin threw open a door. "But there are holes in the shutters, and we don't want the neighbors to see a light. So we'll set the candle on the stairs. There!"

With those words he placed the candle on a flight of stairs opposite the door. He led the way into the room, which was empty except for a broken armchair and an old couch. The stranger sat down on the couch with the air of a weary man. Fagin drew up the armchair so they sat face-to-face. The candle threw a feeble light on the opposite wall.
They spoke for some time in whispers. The stranger appeared to be in a state of considerable irritation.
"I tell you again, the robbery was badly planned," the man said, raising his voice a little. "Why didn't you keep Oliver here and make him a pickpocket?"
"I couldn't have done that even if I'd wanted to, my dear Monks." For it was indeed Monks whom Fagin was addressing.

"Haven't you turned dozens of other boys into pickpockets?" Monks demanded sternly. "If you were patient for a year at most, you could get Oliver convicted. Then he'd be sent safely out of the country, perhaps for life."
"I saw it was not easy to train him in the business," the old man explained. "He was not like other boys in the same circumstances."
"Curse him, no! Or he would have been a thief long ago," muttered Monks.

"I had no hold upon Oliver to make him worse," continued Fagin, anxiously watching the face of his companion. "I had nothing to frighten him with, which I always must have in the beginning or I labor in vain. What could I do? Send him out with the Dodger and Charley? We saw how well that worked. I trembled in fear for us all when he was caught."
" That was not my doing," observed Monks.

"No, no, my dear. And I don't quarrel with it now because if it had never happened, you might never have spotted him when he was arrested. But I got him back for you by using Nancy. And then she began to grow fond of him."
"Get rid of the girl!" Monks said impatiently.

"That sort of thing is not our way. But don't worry," Fagin added with a smile. "I know how these girls are, Monks. As soon as the boy begins to harden, Nancy will care no more for him than for a block of wood. You want him turned into a thief. If he's alive, I can do it this time."
Fagin drew nearer to Monks. "But if worst comes to worst and he's dead . . ."

"It's no fault of mine if he is!" Monks grasped Fagin's arm with trembling hands and a look of terror. "Be careful, Fagin. I told you from the first that I won't shed blood. Anything but his death! If he was shot dead in that robbery, I was not the cause." Monks paused. "What's that?"
"What?" cried Fagin as he sprung to his feet. "Where?"
"There!" Monks pointed to the opposite wall. "A shadow! I saw the shadow of a woman in a cloak and bonnet."

They rushed from the room. The candle, still standing where it had been placed, showed them only the empty staircase and their own white faces. They listened intently, but a profound silence reigned throughout the house.
"It's your imagination," said Fagin, taking up the candle and turning to Monks.
"I swear I saw a shadow," replied Monks, trembling. "It was bending forward when I first saw it, and when I spoke, it darted away."
Fagin glanced contemptuously at Monks. "Follow me, if you please."

They ascended the stairs to the third floor. They looked into all the rooms, but each one was cold, bare, and empty. They descended to the first floor and then to the kitchen below. The green mold hung upon the low walls, but all was still as death.
"What do you think now?" asked Fagin after they had returned to the hall by the front door. "Besides ourselves, there's not a creature in the house except Toby and the boys."

Monks shook his head and laughed grimly, saying it must have been his imagination. Then he declined to continue talking about Oliver because it was now past one o'clock. And so he went out into the cold night.

After Bill Sikes and Toby Crackit had abandoned him, Oliver lay unconscious in the ditch until early morning. At last a low cry of pain broke the stillness. It was the day after the robbery and Oliver was awakening.

His left arm, crudely bandaged in a shawl, hung heavy at his side. He was so weak that he could scarcely sit up. When he had done so, he looked feebly around for help. Trembling from cold and exhaustion, he made an effort to stand but fell back onto the ground.

For a while he remained unconscious, but something within warned him that if he stayed there, he would surely die. So he struggled to his feet and stumbled forward. Staggering on, he crept over fences and through hedges until he came to a road. Here the rain began to fall so heavily that it roused him. He looked up and saw a house not far away. Perhaps the occupants would have pity on him and take him in.

As he drew nearer, he felt that he had seen the house before. But where? Suddenly he remembered. It was the very house they had attempted to rob! Oliver knew he must flee, but he could scarcely stand. He climbed the front steps, knocked faintly at the door, and, with his strength failing him, sank down against a porch pillar.
At that moment the two male servants who had gone out in pursuit of Oliver were entertaining the cook and the housemaid with the story of the previous night's adventures.
"It was about half-past two when I woke up," said Mr. Giles, the butler, sipping tea in the kitchen. "I heard a noise."
"What kind of noise?" asked the cook.
"A noise like somebody was forcing open a door or a window. I decided to wake up Brittles and save him from being murdered in his bed."
Here everyone looked at Brittles, who was still called the lad-of-all-work even though he was over thirty years old.
"I tossed off my bedclothes," said Mr. Giles. "Then I got softly out of bed, put on a pair of—"
"There are ladies present, Mr. Giles," warned Brittles.

"A pair of shoes ." Mr. Giles turned to him and laid great emphasis on the word. "Then I seized the loaded pistol that I always take upstairs at night. I walked on tiptoes to Brittles' room. 'Brittles,' I said when I woke him, 'don't be frightened.'"
" Was he frightened?" asked the cook.
"Not a bit," replied Mr. Giles.
"I would have died at once if it had been me," observed the housemaid.
"You're a woman," said Brittles.
"Brittles is right." Mr. Giles nodded his head approvingly. "Nothing else is to be expected from a woman. But being men, we took a lantern and groped our way downstairs."
Mr. Giles had risen from his chair and taken two steps forward to demonstrate their actions when a sound startled everyone in the kitchen. The cook and the housemaid screamed.
"It was a knock at the front door," said Mr. Giles, perfectly calm. "Open the door, somebody."
Nobody moved.
"A knock coming so early in the morning seems strange. But somebody must open the door."
Mr. Giles looked at Brittles, who said nothing.
"If Brittles would prefer to open the door in the presence of witnesses, I will be one," said Mr. Giles.

Brittles went upstairs, followed by Mr. Giles and the two women, who were too frightened to stay behind in the kitchen. They talked loudly to warn any evil person outside that they were strong in number.
Brittles opened the door while the others peeked over his shoulders. And there sat poor little Oliver Twist.
"A boy!" exclaimed Mr. Giles, pushing Brittles aside. "Why, Brittles, do you know who this is?"
Mr. Giles grabbed Oliver and lugged him into the front hall.
"Here's one of the thieves, ma'am!" Mr. Giles called up the staircase. "He's wounded, miss! I shot him and Brittles held the light."

The two female servants ran upstairs to carry the news to old Mrs. Maylie, the owner of the house, and her niece, Rose. Mr. Giles tried to revive Oliver so that he wouldn't die before he could be hanged.
In the midst of all this commotion, a sweet female voice quieted everything in an instant.
"Giles!" whispered Rose, a pretty young woman.
"Don't be frightened, miss. He didn't make a very desperate resistance. I was soon too much for him."
"Hush!" replied the young lady. "You frighten my aunt as much as the thieves did. Is the poor creature badly hurt?"
"Wounded desperately."
"He looks as if he is dying, miss," called Brittles. "Would you like to come and look at him in case he does?"

Rose preferred to consult with her aunt. She soon returned to the top of the stairs with the instructions that the wounded person was to be carried carefully up to Mr. Giles' room. Brittles was ordered to ride to Chertsey and send for the doctor and a policeman.
"Poor fellow!" said Rose as she refused yet another offer to look at the thief. "Oh, treat him kindly, Giles, for my sake."
An hour later Dr. Losberne bustled into the room where Rose and her aunt were finishing breakfast.
"My dear Mrs. Maylie! I never heard of such a thing! Breaking into a house in the middle of the night!" exclaimed the doctor. "You ought to be dead with fright! And you, Miss Rose—"
"Yes, indeed," said Rose, interrupting him. "But there is a poor creature upstairs whom my aunt wishes you to see."
"Ah, to be sure. Lead me to him, Giles. This was your handiwork, I understand."
The doctor followed the butler upstairs.

The doctor was absent much longer than either he or the ladies had anticipated. The servants ran up and down the stairs as a large box was fetched out of his carriage and the bedroom bell was rung very often. At last Dr. Losberne rejoined Rose and Mrs. Maylie.
"This is a very extraordinary thing," he said. "Have you seen the thief?"
"No," said Mrs. Maylie.
"Then you should come with me at once." He offered one arm to Rose and held out his other hand to Mrs. Maylie. "I promise there's nothing alarming in his appearance."
Leading them upstairs, he paused for a moment outside the bedroom. Then he threw open the door.
"Oh, my!" said Mrs. Maylie.
"He's only a boy!" gasped Rose.
Rose sat by the boy's bed and smoothed his hair away from his face. As she bent over him, her tears fell upon his forehead. The boy stirred and smiled in his sleep.
"This poor child couldn't have been the pupil of robbers!" exclaimed Mrs. Maylie.
Dr. Losberne sighed. "It's possible."
"But at so early an age?" Rose protested.
The doctor mournfully shook his head. "Crime, like death, is not confined to the old."

"But even if he has been wicked, he may never have known a mother's love or the comfort of a home," said Rose. "Hunger may have driven him to live with evil men who turned him to crime." Then she turned to Mrs. Maylie. "Dear aunt, think what might have become of me if you hadn't taken me in. Oh, have pity on him!"
Mrs. Maylie hugged Rose. "Do you think I would harm him? What can I do to save him, Dr. Losberne?"
"The boy will soon wake," said the doctor. "I propose that I question him in front of you. If he's truly bad, he shall be left to his fate. But if he's good, I'll intervene for him."

Oliver was very ill and weak from loss of blood. Yet he managed to tell the sad story of his life, and everyone was moved by it. Rose's gentle hands smoothed Oliver's pillow. He felt calm and happy as he fell back to sleep.
Dr. Losberne went down to the kitchen. He found Mr. Giles and Brittles entertaining the servants and the policeman again with the story of the robbery.
"How is the patient, sir?" asked Mr. Giles.
"So-so," replied the doctor. "Can you and Brittles swear that the boy upstairs is the boy who was put through the window last night? Come on, out with it!"
The doctor, who was normally quite kind and patient, made this demand in a dreadful tone of anger. Giles and Brittles stared at each other.
"Pay great attention to their reply," Dr. Losberne said sharply to the policeman. "It's a simple question of identity."
"That's what it is indeed, sir," replied the policeman.

"A house is broken into," said Dr. Losberne. "A couple of men catch a glimpse of a boy in the darkness. The next morning a boy comes to the house. And because he has his arm bandaged, they grab him and swear he is the thief."
The policeman nodded wisely.
"I ask you again," thundered the doctor. "Are you, on your solemn oaths, able to identify that boy?"

Brittles looked doubtfully at Mr. Giles, and Mr. Giles looked doubtfully at Brittles. The policeman put his hand behind his ear the better to hear the reply. The two female servants leaned forward . . .
And just then there was a knock at the front door.
"It's the detectives from London!" cried Brittles, appearing much relieved.
"The what?" exclaimed the doctor.
"The London detectives, sir," said Brittles. "We sent for them this morning."
Brittles went upstairs and opened the door. Two men stood there. One was stout with black hair, and the other was thin with red hair. Brittles led them into the parlor.
"Tell your master that Blathers and Duff are here," said the stout man, laying a pair of handcuffs on a table. "Oh! Good evening, master. Can I have a word with you in private?"
Blathers addressed this remark to the doctor, who had entered the parlor with the two ladies. Dr. Losberne dismissed Brittles.
"This is the lady of the house," said Dr. Losberne, motioning toward Mrs. Maylie. Then he proceeded to tell the story of the attempted robbery.
"I can't say for certain until I've examined the evidence," said Blathers, "but I don't think this was done by local people."
"Certainly not," said Duff.
"Who is this boy that the servants are talking about?" asked Blathers.
"One of the frightened servants took it into his head that the boy had something to do with the robbery. But it's nonsense, sheer absurdity," said Dr. Losberne.
"Where did this boy come from? He didn't drop out of the clouds, did he?" asked Blathers.
"Of course not," replied the doctor with a nervous glance at the two ladies. "I know his whole history, but first wouldn't you like to see where the thieves made their attempt?"
"Certainly," replied Blathers. "We should inspect the premises first and examine the servants afterward. That's the usual way of doing business."

So everyone went off to examine the little window, where the thieves had gained entry to the house. Then while the detectives interviewed the servants in the kitchen, the doctor paced the parlor in an uneasy state. Mrs. Maylie and Rose looked on with anxious faces.
"I hardly know what to do," said Dr. Losberne.
"Surely the poor child's story will be enough to show he's innocent," said Rose.

"I doubt it, my dear," said Dr. Losberne. "He admits that he has been the companion of thieves for quite some time. He was arrested on a pickpocket charge. Violent men brought him here to rob the house . . ."
"Oh, why did the servants send for the detectives?" cried Rose.
"We cannot let these men know the boy's real story," Dr. Losberne said firmly.
The detectives soon returned. Blathers announced that the robbers were probably two men from the city, who used a boy to climb through the window. He insisted on seeing Oliver.
Holding a candle, Mr. Giles led the detectives upstairs to Oliver's bedside. Dr. Losberne followed with Rose and Mrs. Maylie.

"This lad was wounded by a trap meant for poachers." Dr. Losberne helped Oliver to sit up in bed. "He was trespassing near here and came to the house for help this morning. Mr. Giles immediately grabbed him and put the boy's life in danger. Do you deny that, Giles?"
"It was all done for the best, sir." Mr. Giles was bewildered. "I thought it was the robbers' boy."
"Well, do you think so now?" asked Blathers.
"I don't know. I really don't know." Mr. Giles shook his head. "I couldn't swear it's him."
"You're a muddle-headed chap," said Duff.
Dr. Losberne suggested they ask the same question of Brittles. But Brittles was no more certain of the boy's identity than Mr. Giles had been.
"It could be the same boy," said Brittles. "But it might not be. I only thought it was the same boy because Mr. Giles said it was."
At last Blathers shook his head in disgust. "There is no robber here," he pronounced.
Oliver's ailments were neither slight nor few. Besides his wounded arm, he suffered from a fever, which gave him aches and chills and hung on for many weeks. But at last he began to get better.
Sometimes he told Rose and Mrs. Maylie, in a few tearful words, how much he appreciated what they had done for him. He wished he could do something to show his gratitude.

"Poor fellow," said Rose one day when he was thanking her. "You will have many opportunities to serve us if you want. We are soon going to the country. The quiet place, the pure air, and the beauties of spring will restore you in a few days. We will employ you in a hundred ways when you are strong enough to work."
"Oh, dear lady," cried Oliver. "If only I could work for you now. If only I could give you pleasure by watering your flowers or running errands!"

"You will make me happier than I can tell you," replied Rose. "I'm already happy that my good aunt rescued you from such a miserable life. But it makes me even happier to know that you're grateful. Do you understand me?" she asked, watching Oliver's thoughtful face.
"Oh yes, miss, yes," Oliver replied eagerly. "I was just thinking that I am being ungrateful now."
"To whom?" inquired Rose.
"To the kind gentleman and his dear old housekeeper who took such good care of me before. I'm sure they would be pleased to know how happy I am."
"I'm sure they would. In fact, Dr. Losberne has already promised that he will take you to see them soon."
"He has?" Oliver's face brightened with pleasure. "I don't know what I'll do when I see their kind faces again."

In a short time, Oliver was well enough to undertake the trip to Mr. Brownlow's house. One morning he and Dr. Losberne set out in a coach that belonged to Mrs. Maylie. Soon after passing through Chertsey, Oliver suddenly turned very pale and uttered a loud exclamation.
"What's the matter?" cried the doctor, all in a bustle as usual. "Do you see anything? Hear anything? Feel anything? Eh?"
"That, sir!" cried Oliver, pointing out the carriage window. "That house!"
"Yes, what about it? Stop, coachman. Pull up here!" cried Dr. Losberne. "What about the house?"
"The robber . . . Bill Sikes," whispered Oliver. "That's the house he took me to, where we met the other robber."
"It is? Let me out, coachman."
But before the coachman could climb down, Dr. Losberne had rushed out of the coach. Running over to the deserted house, he began kicking at the door.
"Hello? What's the matter?" A little hunchbacked man opened the door so suddenly that the doctor almost fell into the front hall.
"Matter!" exclaimed the doctor, grabbing the man by the collar. "Robbery is the matter."
"Murder will be the matter too, if you don't take your hands off me."
"Where is that robber fellow?" Dr. Losberne demanded. "What's his name? Sikes, that's it. Where's Sikes, you thief?"
The man twisted himself out of the doctor's grasp. He growled some horrid oaths and then retired into the house. But before the man could shut the door, the doctor had followed him in.

Dr. Losberne went into the parlor and looked anxiously around. Nothing matched Oliver's description. Not the room. Not the furniture. He passed into another parlor, which again bore no resemblance whatsoever to Oliver's account of the house.
"What do you want?" screamed the little man.
"The boy must have made a mistake," Dr. Losberne muttered to himself. "Here, put that in your pocket!" With those words he flung some money at the man and hurried out to the carriage.

The man followed him to the carriage door, uttering the wildest curses and exclamations. Spying Oliver, the man gave him a glance so fierce and vindictive that Oliver could not forget it for months afterward. The coachman resumed his seat and they were off. Looking back, Oliver and Dr. Losberne could see the little man stamping his feet and tearing his hair in rage.
"I'm a fool," said Dr. Losberne after a long silence. "Even if it had been the right place and the right fellows had been there, what could I have done by myself?"
The doctor sat brooding for a few minutes but soon returned to his usual good temper. Oliver's replies to his questions were as sincere as ever, so the doctor decided to continue to trust the boy.
Because Oliver knew the name of Mr. Brownlow's street, they were able to drive straight there. When the coach turned into it, Oliver's heart was beating so hard that he could barely breathe.
"Now, my boy, which house is it?" inquired Dr. Losberne.
"That one!" replied Oliver, pointing eagerly out the coach window. "The white one. Oh, hurry. I'm so excited I could die."
"Now, now." The good doctor patted him on the shoulder. "You'll see them soon, and they'll be overjoyed to find you safe and well."
"Oh, I hope so. They were so very good to me."
The coach stopped. No, that was the wrong house. It went on again and stopped. Oliver looked up at the windows with happy tears of expectation running down his face.
Alas, the house was empty with a "For Rent" sign in the window.
Dr. Losberne got out of the coach and took Oliver by the hand. They knocked on the door of the next house. The servant told them that Mr. Brownlow and his staff had left for the West Indies.
Oliver sank feebly backward. Dr. Losberne guided him into the coach.
"Head for home," Dr. Losberne directed the coachman.
"But what about the bookseller?" pleaded Oliver. "I know the way there. Maybe he could tell us more about Mr. Brownlow."
"My poor boy, this is disappointment enough for one day."

Oliver was filled with sorrow. Many times during his illness, he had cheered himself with the thought of greeting Mr. Brownlow and Mrs. Bedwin again. He wanted to thank them. He had been buoyed up by the hope of explaining how he had been snatched away from them. Now they had gone far away, carrying with them the belief that he was an impostor and a robber. He might never have a chance to explain everything to them. Thinking about that was almost too much for Oliver to bear.
A few weeks later, spring arrived. Every tree and flower put forth young leaves and rich blossoms. The Maylies and Oliver left Chertsey for a cottage in the country.

It was a happy time. Every morning Oliver was up by six o'clock, roaming the fields in search of flowers. He returned home laden with blossoms for the breakfast table. Then he went to the village to study with a kind, white-haired gentleman.
In the afternoon he walked with Mrs. Maylie and Rose. Sometimes they sat in a shady place and listened to Rose read aloud. After that Oliver prepared his lesson for the next day.
In the evening they walked out again, and Oliver listened with great pleasure to all that the ladies said. When darkness fell and they returned home, Rose played the piano and sang in a gentle voice.
So three months glided away and spring melted into summer.

One beautiful night they had taken a longer walk than usual. When they returned home, Rose sat down at the piano. After running her hands over the keys, she began to play something solemn. And as she played, Oliver and Mrs. Maylie heard her weeping.
"Rose, my love!" cried Mrs. Maylie, rising hastily and bending over her. "Why are you crying?"
"I don't know," replied the young lady. "I can't describe it, but I feel . . ."
"Not ill, my love?"
"No, not ill." Rose shuddered with cold. "I'll be better soon. Please close the window."
Oliver hurried to comply with her request. Rose tried to play a livelier tune, but her fingers fell powerless on the keys. Covering her face with her hands, she sank onto a sofa and wept.
"I don't want to alarm you, Aunt, but I fear I am ill."
Her face turned as white as marble, yet in another minute, it was flushed. Oliver was alarmed, but Mrs. Maylie tried to stay calm. She urged Rose to retire for the night.
"I hope nothing is the matter," said Oliver when Rose had left the room.
"I hope so too," said Mrs. Maylie. "But I fear I may be in danger of losing the dear girl."
"Surely there is no danger of anything so dreadful? She was quite well two hours ago."
"She's very ill now and will be worse, I'm sure. My dear, dear Rose. What would I do without her?"
Oliver did not know what to say. He could not bear to think of Rose dying.
An anxious night passed. The next morning Rose had a high and dangerous fever.

"We must take action, Oliver." Mrs. Maylie handed him a letter for Dr. Losberne. "This letter must be carried to the market town, four miles away. Then it should be taken by horseback to Chertsey. The people at the inn will know how to do this."
Oliver put the letter in his pocket.
"Here's another letter," said Mrs. Maylie, hesitating a bit. "But I don't know whether to send it now or wait until I see if Rose worsens."
"Is it for Chertsey too, ma'am?" Oliver held out his trembling hand.
"No," replied Mrs. Maylie, giving it to him mechanically.
Oliver glanced at the envelope and saw it was addressed to Harry Maylie at some great lord's house.
"Shall it go too?" Oliver asked.
"I think not," replied Mrs. Maylie, taking back the letter. "I'll wait until tomorrow."
With these words she gave Oliver her purse, and he started off. Swiftly he ran across the fields and down the little lanes. Now and then he stopped for a few seconds to catch his breath.

At last he arrived, hot and covered with dust, at the market town. Looking around, he spotted the large house that was the inn. He spoke to a boy, who had been dozing at the gate. The boy referred him to the landlord, who was leaning against the stable door.

The landlord walked slowly into the inn to make out a bill for delivering the letter, and he was gone a long time. After the bill was ready and Oliver had paid it with the money from Mrs. Maylie's purse, a horse had to be saddled and a man had to get ready. Meanwhile Oliver was in a desperate state of impatience and anxiety. If he could, he would have jumped on the horse himself and ridden away.
At last the letter was on its way, and Oliver hurried out to the innyard with a somewhat lighter heart. He stumbled against a tall man, wrapped in a dark cloak, who was coming out the inn door.
"Hah! What's this?" cried the man, fixing his eyes on Oliver and jumping back in surprise.
"I beg your pardon, sir," said Oliver. "I was in a great hurry to get home and didn't see you."
"Death to you!" cried the man in a horrible passion. "If only I'd had the courage to say the word, I could have been free of you. What are you doing here?"
The man shook his fist at Oliver and advanced toward him as if he wanted to strike the startled boy. But before that could happen, the man fell violently to the ground, writhing in a fit.
Oliver darted into the inn for help. Once the man was carried safely inside, Oliver ran as fast as he could to make up for lost time. All the way home, he thought of the strange, menacing man.
But once he reached the cottage, there were more pressing things to think about. Rose had grown worse. In fact, a local medical practitioner said it would be a miracle if she recovered.
The next day visitors came and went, speaking in hushed voices. Late at night Dr. Losberne finally arrived.
"There is very little hope," he announced after examining Rose.
Oliver's heart sank.

The next morning Oliver went out to walk in the fields. It was a beautiful, sunny day with a sense of peace and beauty in the landscape. Oliver turned homeward, thinking of Rose and the many kindnesses he had received from her.
When he reached home, Mrs. Maylie was sitting in the parlor.
"She is in a deep sleep, Oliver," said the grieving old woman. "Dr. Losberne says she will either recover or never wake up again."
Oliver sat down next to Mrs. Maylie on the sofa. He held her hand, and there they sat for hours, refusing all food and afraid to speak. Together they watched as the sun sank lower and lower.
At sunset Dr. Losberne entered the parlor, where Oliver and Mrs. Maylie had been sitting for hours.
"Tell me at once!" cried Mrs. Maylie, rising from the couch. "Is Rose dead?"
"Compose yourself, dear ma'am," said the doctor. "Rose has survived, and she will live to bless us all for years to come."
The good news was almost too much to bear. Mrs. Maylie sank with relief into Dr. Losberne's arms. Oliver was stunned. He could not weep or speak or remain in that room for one moment longer.

He went out for a long, rambling walk in the evening air. At last he burst into tears of relief. Wiping his eyes, he began to gather flowers for Rose. The night was closing in as he headed homeward, his arms laden with a huge bouquet.
As he walked along the road, he heard the sound of a carriage approaching from behind. It dashed past him, and he caught a glimpse of a familiar face. Mr. Giles!
The carriage came to a halt, and the butler stuck his head out the window.
"Oliver!" cried Mr. Giles. "How is Miss Rose?"
Oliver ran up to the coach. A young gentleman pushed Mr. Giles aside and addressed Oliver. "Is she better or worse?"
"Better. Much better, sir!" said Oliver.
"Are you sure?" The gentleman jumped out of the carriage and took Oliver by the arm.
"I'm quite sure, sir. Dr. Losberne says that she's out of danger."

The gentleman turned his face away and remained silent for some moments. Oliver thought he heard the man sobbing while Mr. Giles sat on the carriage steps, wiping his eyes with a blue handkerchief dotted with white spots.
"You go ahead to my mother's house, Giles," said the young man. "I'd rather walk to gain a little time before I see her."

"I beg your pardon, Mr. Harry, but I'd like to walk with you." Mr. Giles gave his face one final wipe with the handkerchief. "It wouldn't be proper for the staff to see me in this state. I'd never have any authority over them if they did."
Harry Maylie smiled. "You may do as you like." So the three of them walked slowly toward the cottage.
Mrs. Maylie was anxiously waiting for her son when he arrived.
"Mother!" said the young man as they embraced. "Why didn't you write to me sooner?"
"I did. But then I decided not to send the letter until Dr. Losberne had seen Rose."
"But what if she had died?" chided Harry. "You know I love her!"
"I know that she deserves the best love that a man can offer. And now I must say something that it pains me to say." Mrs. Maylie paused. "Sometimes a young man's love doesn't last."
"That is unkind, Mother."

"Rose has a stain upon her name, Harry. She's illegitimate. And you're ambitious, which means people will sneer at her." Mrs. Maylie fixed her eyes on her son's face. "If you marry her, you may live to regret your decision. And seeing your regret will only hurt Rose."
"Are you going to oppose my marriage?" asked Harry.
"I won't, but I'd like you to consider—"

"I have considered these things for years and years," Harry said impatiently. "My feelings remain unchanged, and they always will. There is no point in remaining silent. Before I leave this place, Rose will hear me."
"Yes, she will hear you," Mrs. Maylie echoed flatly.
"You sound as if she will hear my offer of marriage but not accept me. Has she fallen in love with someone else?" Harry demanded.
"No indeed. You have a strong hold on her affections. But think of her history. Her awareness of her situation may influence her decision. Devoted as she is to us, she can be self-sacrificing."
"What do you mean?"
"I leave that to you to discover," replied Mrs. Maylie. "I must go back to her now."
"You will tell her I am here?" said Harry.
"Of course."
"And say how anxious I have been and how I long to see her? You will not refuse to do this, Mother?"
"No, I will tell her everything." Pressing her son's hand affectionately, Mrs. Maylie left the room.

Harry was soon able to see Rose for himself. But he knew that now was not the time to talk of marriage. That would have to wait until she was better. In the meantime he went out every morning with Oliver to pick flowers for her.

The days flew by, and Rose was rapidly recovering. She was still confined to her bed, so there were no evening walks. But Oliver was not idle. He applied himself to his studies and surprised himself with how much he learned.
The little room where he studied was on the ground floor at the back of the house. The window overlooked a garden, and beyond that lay fine meadowland and woods.
One warm evening at twilight, Oliver sat reading in this room. He had been poring over his books for some time and began to grow drowsy. Gradually he fell asleep.

There is a kind of sleep in which the person is still conscious of sounds and things going on around him. That is the state that Oliver was in. He knew perfectly well that he was in his own little room and that his books were lying on the table before him. And yet he was asleep.

Suddenly the scene changed, and the air became dank and heavy. He thought, with a shudder of terror, that he was in Fagin's house again. The hideous old man sat in his usual corner of the kitchen, pointing at Oliver and whispering to another man.
Oliver thought he heard Fagin say, "Hush, my dear! It's the boy, sure enough. Come away."
"That boy!" the other man seemed to answer. "I'd recognize him anywhere."
The man seemed to say this with such dreadful hatred that Oliver woke up. He couldn't move. He couldn't speak because there—right there at the window—stood Fagin!

Fagin was so close that Oliver could have almost touched him. And standing beside him, white with fear or rage or both, was the man from the inn—the angry man in the dark cloak who had threatened Oliver! A red scar marred the man's neck.
The two men were at the window for only an instant, and then they were gone. But they had recognized Oliver, and he had recognized them.
Oliver stood transfixed for a moment. Then, leaping from the window into the garden, he called loudly for help.
Hearing Oliver's shouts, Harry Maylie and Mr. Giles rushed outside. They found Oliver, pale and agitated, pointing toward the meadows behind the house.
"Fagin! Fagin!" cried Oliver.
Mr. Giles had no idea what this name meant. But Harry had heard Oliver's story from his mother, so he knew who Fagin was.
"Where did he go?" Harry picked up a large stick.
"There!" Oliver pointed in the direction that Fagin had taken.
"Then he must be in the ditch! Follow me!" Harry sprang over a hedge, with Mr. Giles and Oliver trying to keep up with him. Dr. Losberne, who was just returning from a walk, joined the chase.

At last they reached the ditch, but no one was hiding in it. They walked to the top of a little hill. From there they could see all the open fields for several miles around. The village lay in one direction and the woods in another. But Fagin could not have reached either place without their spotting him.
"It must have been a dream, Oliver," said Harry.
"Oh no, sir." Oliver shuddered at the memory of Fagin's face. "I saw him too plainly for that. I saw them both as plainly as I see you now."
"Both?" said Dr. Losberne.
"Who was the other person?" asked Harry.
"A strange man who shouted at me the day I took Mrs. Maylie's letter to the inn."
"Are you sure they went this way?" Harry demanded.
Oliver insisted, and the others wanted to believe him. But there were no footprints or any other sign of the two men.

Harry sent Mr. Giles to ask about the two men at the village. No one had seen them. The next day Oliver and Harry went to the inn at the market town, hoping to hear something about the men there. This effort was equally fruitless, and in a few days, everyone forgot about the whole affair.

Meanwhile Rose continued to recover. She left her room and was able to go outdoors. Cheerful voices and merry laughter could once again be heard in the cottage. But Oliver could not help noticing that something was wrong. Mrs. Maylie and her son were often closeted together for a long time. More than once Rose appeared to have been crying.
At last one morning when Rose was alone in the breakfast room, Harry begged permission to speak to her. Rose turned pale and nodded.
"I was brought here by the fear of losing you." He grasped her hand. "I dreaded that you would die and never know how devotedly I loved you."
Tears came to Rose's eyes.

"My own dear Rose!" Harry went on. "For years I've loved you. I hoped to win my way to fame and then come home and tell you I'd done it only for you. Alas, I am not famous. But I offer you my heart, which you have long possessed. Will you marry me?"
"You have been ever so kind." Rose struggled to hold back her tears. "But I can only be your friend and not your wife."
Harry still held Rose's hand. She covered her face with her other hand and wept.
"And what are your reasons for this decision?" he asked in a low voice.

"There is a stain upon my name," she said. "I cannot bring disgrace to you or to your mother, who has been like a mother to me. I won't have people saying that I married you to enhance my name and raise my position in the world."
"If I'd been poor or sick, would you have turned me down?" asked Harry.
Rose did not want to answer this question, but Harry pressed her to reply.
"If you'd been even a little above me and I could have helped you, then we could have been happy. But now I'd only ruin your chances among ambitious and distinguished people. Farewell, Harry."
Rose withdrew her hand from his.
"Oh, Rose!" Harry cried. "Promise me one thing. Permit me to speak to you again on this subject in a year. And then I will never mention it again."
"I'll promise you that," Rose said sadly, "although it will be useless to try to persuade me to marry you."
She held out her hand again, but Harry embraced her instead and then hurried from the room.
The next day Harry joined Oliver and Dr. Losberne at the breakfast table.

"So you're going to be my traveling companion today," the doctor said to Harry. "Yesterday you were going to stay here and accompany your mother to the seaside. Then last night you urged, with great mystery, that we start out this morning before the ladies arise. What's going on?"
"I simply changed my mind." Harry studied his tea.
"Why? Have you heard something from those who have been encouraging you to run for Parliament?"
"No. It's unlikely I'd hear anything at this time of year."
"Well, you're an odd fellow," said the doctor. "But I know there are people working to get you into Parliament in the election before Christmas."
"We shall see," Harry mumbled, not wanting to say anything more.
The coach pulled up to the door. Mr. Giles came in for the baggage, and the doctor bustled out to see that it was loaded properly.
"Oliver," said Harry in a low voice. "You can write well now?"
Oliver looked up in surprise. "Yes, sir."
"I won't be home again for some time. I wish you'd write to me every other week. Will you do that?"
"Oh certainly, sir. I'll be proud to do it."
"I'd like to know how my mother and Miss Rose are. You can tell me about the walks you take and what you talk about. And whether she—I mean they—seem happy and well. Do you understand?"
"Oh yes," replied Oliver.
"I'd rather you didn't mention this to the ladies because it might upset my mother," Harry said hurriedly. "Remember to tell me everything. I'm depending on you."
Oliver was pleased and honored by his request.
Harry went outside to join Dr. Losberne. As Harry jumped into the coach, he cast a last glance up at one of the cottage windows.
Jingling and clattering, the coach pulled away in a cloud of dust. But there was one person whose eyes remained fixed on the spot where the coach had disappeared.
"Harry seems happy," Rose said to herself as she sat at the upstairs window. "I'm very glad of that." But tears ran down her face.

Two months had passed since Mr. Bumble had married Mrs. Corney, the matron of the workhouse. Mr. Bumble had become the master of the workhouse, but he was unhappy. He no longer wore the gold-lace trimmed coat and the cocked hat of the parish officer. And he quarreled constantly with the new Mrs. Bumble.

"I was misled by six teaspoons, a pair of sugar tongs, a small quantity of secondhand furniture, and twenty pounds in cash," Mr. Bumble said to himself. "We've been married only a short time, but it seems like forever."
He had just had another argument with his wife. Snatching up his hat, he left the workhouse in a hurry. He roamed the streets until it began to rain heavily. Then he stepped inside a pub.

Mr. Bumble went into the parlor to enjoy his drink and read the newspaper. There was only one other person sitting at the table: a tall man, wearing a dark cloak. The man's clothes were dusty, as if he'd traveled a great distance.
As Mr. Bumble read the newspaper, he couldn't resist stealing a look at the stranger. And every time he did, the stranger was looking at him!
Finally the man said, "I think I've seen you before. You used to be the parish officer, didn't you?"
"Yes," said Mr. Bumble in surprise.
The stranger stood up and closed the door so no one would overhear him.
"I came to this place today to find you. I want some information, and I'm willing to pay for it." He pushed some coins across the table.
The master of the workhouse carefully examined the coins to be sure that they were genuine. Then he put them in his pocket.
"Cast your mind back to the workhouse about ten or twelve years ago," said the stranger. "A boy was born there one night."
"Many boys were. How can you expect me to remember just one?"
"I'm talking about a meek-looking, pale boy, who was apprenticed to an undertaker. He later ran away to London."
"Why, you mean Oliver Twist!" said Mr. Bumble. "I remember him, of course. There wasn't a worse rascal in the work—"
"I don't want to hear about him," interrupted the stranger. "I've heard enough of him. I want to know about the old woman who took care of his mother. Where is she?"
"You're talking about old Sally," said Mr. Bumble. "She died last winter."
The stranger sat lost in thought for a few minutes. Mr. Bumble couldn't tell if he was relieved or disappointed.
"It doesn't matter," the stranger said at last. With that, he rose as if to depart.

But Mr. Bumble saw an opportunity to make some more money. He remembered how agitated his wife had been on the night that Sally died. Although he didn't know everything Sally had told Mrs. Bumble, he knew it concerned Oliver.
"There's one woman who might be able to help you," he said.
The stranger's face seemed to fill with fear. "How can I find her?"
"You'll have to go through me."
The stranger wrote out an address on a scrap of paper and handed it to Mr. Bumble. "Bring her to me tomorrow night at nine o'clock."
After that the two men left the pub, heading in opposite directions. But Mr. Bumble soon realized he needed one more piece of information and hurried after the stranger.
"What do you want?" cried the man, whirling around.
"What name am I to ask for tomorrow night?"
"Monks!" The man strode hastily away.

The sky was dull and overcast when Mr. and Mrs. Bumble set out the next night. The clouds, which had been threatening all day, were spread out densely, as if preparing for a violent thunderstorm. The Bumbles were both wrapped in shabby outer garments that would protect them from the rain and keep them from being recognized.
They headed toward some run-down houses bordering the river. The people who lived there survived by theft and other crimes. Among these houses stood an old factory building.
"This should be the place," said Mr. Bumble, consulting the scrap of paper in his hand.
"Hello!" cried a voice from above. "I'll be down in a minute."
"Is that the man?" Mrs. Bumble asked.
Her husband nodded.
"Then say as little as you can until we find out what he wants."
Monks opened the door, motioned for them to come in quickly, and then shut the door. "Is this the woman?"
Mr. Bumble only nodded, remembering his wife's warning.
Suddenly there was a crack of thunder. Monks turned away for a few minutes. When he looked at them again, his face was distorted and discolored.
"These fits come over me now and then," he said. "Thunder sometimes brings them on."
A lantern cast a dim light. Monks motioned for them to sit down. Mr. Bumble looked nervously around, but Mrs. Bumble was calm.
"Let's get down to business," Monks said to Mrs. Bumble. "Were you with Oliver's mother the night she died?"
"Yes."
"Something was taken from her. Something that she wore . . ."
"What's the information worth to you?" Mrs. Bumble interrupted.
"It could be twenty pounds; it could be nothing."
"I know I have what you want. Make it twenty-five pounds."
"Twenty-five?" Monks pulled away. "What if your information is useless?"
"You can easily take the money from me. I'm alone and unprotected here."
"Not alone, my dear, nor unprotected," Mr. Bumble said in a voice trembling with fear.
Monks removed a canvas bag from his pocket and laid twenty-five pounds on the table. Mrs. Bumble began her story.
"Sally told me she stole a gold necklace from Oliver's mother. She sold it to a pawn shop, but she told me where to find the pawn ticket. I redeemed the necklace, and . . . here it is."

Mrs. Bumble held out a gold locket. Monks pried it open with trembling hands. Inside were two locks of hair and a wedding ring. The locket was inscribed Agnes, with space left for a last name. There was also a date, which was about a year before Oliver was born.
"Is this what you wanted from me?" asked Mrs. Bumble.
"It is," said Monks. "And now I must destroy this evidence of Oliver's past."

He suddenly wheeled the table aside and pulled up a trapdoor in the floor. The three of them looked down at the river swirling angrily below. Monks took a deep breath and then threw the locket into the river.
It was seven o'clock the next evening, but Bill Sikes was just waking from a nap. He had been gravely ill for weeks.
"How do you feel tonight, Bill?" Nancy sat sewing in a corner while the white dog sat loyally next to Sikes' bed.
"Weak, very weak. Hurry up now. Help me out of bed."
Nancy had just settled Bill into a chair when there was a knock at the door. In walked Fagin, Charley Bates, and the Dodger.
"What evil wind blew you here, Fagin?" asked Bill.
"No evil wind at all, my dear. Dodger, open the bundle and give Bill the trifles we spent all our money on."
The Dodger opened the bundle to reveal a rabbit pie, some strong tea, some sugar, and a bottle of wine.
Sikes did not seem impressed. "I need some money tonight, Fagin."
"I don't have a single coin with me," Fagin replied.
"You have lots at home."
"Well, I could send the Dodger home to get—"
"No, no," Sikes interrupted. "He'd forget to come back. Nancy will go with you."

So Nancy soon found herself at Fagin's, waiting for him to count out some coins. Suddenly they heard footsteps in the hall. Just as Fagin went to the door, it was opened by a man in a dark cloak. Monks!
"Who's this?" Monks pointed at Nancy.
"Just one of my young people," said Fagin.
Monks stared at her and then said to Fagin, "I need to speak to you in private."

Fagin led him to a room upstairs. Nancy waited a few moments and then she quietly followed them. She stood outside the room, eavesdropping on their conversation. When she heard them push back their chairs, she ran softly downstairs.
"Are you all right?" Fagin asked her after Monks had left. "You look quite pale."
Nancy looked at the floor and didn't answer his question. "Bill will be angry if I don't return soon. Do you have the money?"
Fagin handed her some coins, and she went back to Bill Sikes.
The next night Nancy added something to Sikes' drink to make him sleep so she could go out for a few hours.
"It will take me at least an hour to walk there," she muttered as she set out.

When she reached the wealthy part of London, the clock was striking eleven. At last she came to her destination: a small hotel on a quiet street. Nancy knew she didn't belong in this posh area, but she squared her shoulders and pushed open the door.
"Who do you want?" said the porter. He gave her a critical look.
"A lady staying here. Miss Rose Maylie."
"And who shall I say is calling?"
"My name won't mean anything to her. I must speak to her myself."
The porter grumbled, but he found a boy to take a message to Rose. Meanwhile he led Nancy into a room to wait. At last the door opened and a beautiful young woman entered the room.
"I am Rose Maylie," said the young woman, looking at Nancy's ragged clothes. "What can I do for you? If you're in poverty or in trouble, I'll try my best to help you. Please sit down."
"Let me stand. I'm about to put my life and the lives of others in your hands." Nancy began to weep. "I'm the one who dragged Oliver back to Fagin when he was on his way to the bookseller's."
"You!" Rose was shocked.
"I've sneaked away from people who would surely murder me if they knew I'd come here to tell you something. Do you know a man named Monks?"
"No," said Rose.
"He knows you, and he knew you were staying here. That's how I found you."
Rose was alarmed. "But who is he?"

"Someone who knows Fagin. Soon after Oliver arrived at your house, I overheard a conversation between Monks and Fagin. Monks accidentally saw Oliver on the day we first lost him, the day Oliver was accused of stealing a gentleman's handkerchief."
"Oh yes." Rose nodded. "I remember Oliver telling us that was the day he went to live with Mr. Brownlow."

"Monks had been looking for Oliver, but I don't know why," Nancy went on. "So Monks made a deal with Fagin. Get Oliver back from Mr. Brownlow, and Monks would give Fagin some money. If Fagin could turn Oliver into a criminal, Fagin would receive even more money."
Rose was puzzled. "Why would Monks want Oliver turned into a criminal?"
"I don't know. Monks caught sight of my shadow on the wall that night, and I had to flee the house."
"Did you ever see Monks again?"

"Not until last night when he came to Fagin's. I eavesdropped again when they went upstairs to talk. Monks boasted that he'd tossed in the river the only proof of Oliver's identity. He said that Oliver was his younger brother, and he'd now secured all of their father's inheritance for himself."
"His brother!" exclaimed Rose.

"Those were his words." Nancy glanced uneasily around, fearful that somehow Sikes had managed to follow her. "I must leave now. I have to reach home before anyone suspects that I've been out on an errand such as this."
"No, wait," said Rose. "I can summon a gentleman who will help you. If you repeat this information to him, he'll see that you are sent immediately to a place of safety."
"I want to go home. How can I explain this to you? Among the men that I've described, there is one I can't leave. He's the worst of all, but I love him."
"Oh, don't go back to him!" Tears ran down Rose's face. "You've risked your life for Oliver. Please, let me save you."
Nancy sank to her knees. "Dear, sweet angel. You're the first person who has been kind to me. But it's too late to save me from a life of crime."
"It's never too late."
"It is. If I told anyone else what I've told you, the man I love would be sure to hang. "
Nancy rose and turned toward the door.
"Wait!" said Rose. "Where can I find you if I need to speak to you again?"
"I'll wait for you on London Bridge every Sunday night between eleven o'clock and midnight. That is, if I'm still alive."
"At least take some money from me."
"Not a penny," replied Nancy.
And with a sob, she left the room. Rose sank into a chair, wondering what to do next.

Rose had trouble sleeping that night. She was eager to learn more about the mystery of Oliver's family. But Nancy had come to her in confidence and trusted her with the information that Monks and Oliver were brothers.

Nancy's manner had touched Rose's heart, and Rose hoped that somehow she could help the miserable young woman. But Rose also loved Oliver, and there wasn't much time to help him. Mrs. Maylie, Oliver, and Rose were going to be in London for only two more days. Then they would be traveling to the coast for several weeks.
"I have to make a plan that can be executed in 48 hours!" Rose told herself. She sat up in bed, wide awake. "Or perhaps I can postpone our journey without causing suspicion!"

Dr. Losberne was also staying with them at the London hotel. But Rose was well acquainted with the excellent gentleman's impetuosity. If he learned that Nancy was the one who had captured Oliver for Fagin, he'd scour the city until he found her.

"Then who knows what rash act Dr. Losberne might commit," Rose murmured. "No, I can't tell him. I also can't confide in my aunt because the first thing she'll do is consult Dr. Losberne. Maybe I could write to Harry."
But then she remembered the last time she'd seen Harry, when she'd refused his marriage proposal. Tears came to her eyes. Still uncertain what to do, Rose lay down and finally fell asleep.

The next morning she reluctantly decided to consult Harry. She sat with pen and paper, trying to write, but she couldn't think of what to say. Just then Oliver burst into her room. He had been out walking with Mr. Giles, and his face was flushed.
"What's wrong?" asked Rose in alarm.
"I hardly know where to begin," Oliver said breathlessly. "I've seen him! At last you'll know that I was telling you the truth."
"Who are you talking about?" asked Rose.
"The gentleman who was so good to me. Mr. Brownlow."
"Where did you see him?" Rose laid down her pen, all thoughts of her letter forgotten.
"Getting out of a coach and going into a house. I was trembling so much that I couldn't speak to him. But Mr. Giles asked a servant whether Mr. Brownlow lives there and he does!"
Oliver showed Rose a scrap of paper. "Here's his address. Oh, dear me! What shall I do when I see him?"
"Quick!" said Rose. "Find someone to fetch us a coach and be ready to go with me in a few minutes. I'll tell my aunt that we're going out, but I won't say anything more. Now hurry!"

In just over five minutes, they were on their way to Mr. Brownlow's house. Rose left Oliver in the coach under the pretense of preparing Mr. Brownlow for his arrival. A servant led her upstairs to a room, where Mr. Brownlow was sitting.
"I have some news that will no doubt surprise you," said Rose after Mr. Brownlow had invited her to sit. "You once took an interest in a young friend of mine."
"Indeed, who is that?" Mr. Brownlow was intrigued.
"Oliver Twist."
Mr. Brownlow was astonished to hear that name again. "What has become of him?"
Rose told Mr. Brownlow everything that had happened to Oliver since that fateful day when he left for the bookseller's. But she did not share what Nancy had told her.
"I'm very happy to hear this news of Oliver. Very happy. But you haven't told me where he is now."
"He's waiting in a coach at the door."
"At my door?" cried the old gentleman.
With that he hurried from the room, down the stairs, and into the coach.
"Oliver!" exclaimed Mr. Brownlow. "I knew you'd come back!"
Overcome by tears of happiness, Oliver could not speak, but he embraced Mr. Brownlow. Hand in hand, they returned to the room where Rose was waiting.
"There's someone else whom we should not forget." Mr. Brownlow rang the bell, summoning his housekeeper.
Mrs. Bedwin responded to the bell at once. Dropping a curtsy to Mr. Brownlow, she waited for his orders.
"Can't you see why I've summoned you?" Mr. Brownlow said somewhat crossly. "Put on your glasses."
The old lady rummaged in her pocket. But Oliver could not wait for her to find her glasses. He ran to her and sprang into her arms.
"My innocent boy!" she exclaimed as she hugged him.
"My dear nurse!" cried Oliver.
"I knew you would come back. How well you look! The same sweet face, but not so pale. The same gentle eyes, but not so sad. Where have you been?"
Oliver began to tell his story.
"I must speak to you alone," Rose whispered to Mr. Brownlow.
He led her into another room, where she revealed to him what Nancy had told her. Rose also explained why she could not tell her aunt or Dr. Losberne.
"A wise decision," said Mr. Brownlow. "Leave Dr. Losberne to me. I will call at the hotel this evening at eight o'clock and explain everything to him."
Rose and Oliver soon had to return to the hotel, with Oliver promising to visit Mrs. Bedwin again.
That night Mr. Brownlow met with Dr. Losberne, Mrs. Maylie, and Rose. Oliver was left alone in the next room, so he wouldn't hear what was said.

Dr. Losberne was every bit as angry as Rose had feared. As soon as he heard Nancy's story, he was halfway out the door, threatening to track her down. Somehow Mr. Brownlow managed to stop him from going to the police.
"So what are we supposed to do now?" Dr. Losberne said impatiently.

"We need to find out who Oliver's parents were and discover if Nancy's story is true," said Mr. Brownlow. "Is this man Monks really trying to cheat Oliver out of his inheritance? First we must ask Nancy if she's willing to point out Monks to us so we can deal with him."

"That means we can't meet her until Sunday night—five days away," said Dr. Losberne. "But that will give me time to contact Harry Maylie, who will be a great help to us, I'm sure. He's Mrs. Maylie's son and a dear friend of Rose's."
Rose blushed deeply but didn't say anything.
"We will remain in London, of course," said Mrs. Maylie. "I don't care how long this takes."
Mr. Brownlow stood up. "Now let's go to supper. Poor Oliver probably thinks we've tired of him and are plotting how to get rid of him."

Nancy knew that she had done the right thing by contacting Rose, but a part of her regretted her actions. She felt bitter toward Fagin for leading her into a life of crime. Yet she still didn't want to be the one who brought him within the grasp of the police.

As for Bill Sikes, she had dropped no clues that could lead to his discovery. For his sake she had refused Rose's offers of sanctuary. She had done all she could for Sikes. She had done the right thing for Oliver.
Although she came to this same conclusion whenever she thought about the situation, Nancy still felt uneasy. She quickly grew pale and thin with anxiety.

It was Sunday night at Bill Sikes' house. Nancy sat silent and dejected with her head in her hands. When the clock on the nearest church struck the hour, Nancy raised her head, remembering how she'd told Rose to look for her on London Bridge on Sunday nights.
"It's eleven o'clock," said Sikes. He went to the window and peeked through the shutter. "A dark night too. A good night for some illegal business."
"What a pity, Bill, my dear," said Fagin, "that there's none quite ready to be done. We need to plan another robbery now that you're feeling better."
"Yes, we must make up for lost time," said Sikes.
"It does me good to hear you talk like that." Fagin reached over and patted him on the shoulder. "You're quite like yourself again."
They bantered back and forth, ignoring Nancy. Taking advantage of this, she put on her bonnet and started to go out. But Fagin suddenly noticed her and pulled on Sikes' sleeve.
"Hold on, Nancy!" cried Sikes. "Where are you going at this time of night?"
"Not far."
"What kind of answer is that? Tell me where you're going."
"I don't know where," replied Nancy.
"Then I do. You're going nowhere. Sit down." Sikes said this more out of stubbornness than because he really objected to her going out.
"I'm not well. You know that. I want a breath of air."
"Stick your head out the window."
"I can't get enough air that way. I need to go out on the street."
"You're not going out." Sikes crossed the room and locked the door. Then he pulled Nancy's bonnet from her head and flung it on top of an old chest.
"Lack of a bonnet won't keep me inside," Nancy said angrily. "Do you know what you're doing, Bill?"
"Know what I'm doing?" Sikes turned to Fagin. "She must be out of her senses or she wouldn't dare talk to me that way."
"You'll drive me to something desperate," Nancy threatened. "Let me go this minute!"
"No!" shouted Sikes.
"Tell him to let me go, Fagin," Nancy said pleadingly.
Fagin continued to watch the scene in silence, wondering why Nancy needed to go out right that minute.
"Bill, you really don't know what you're doing!" Nancy said with great force. Then she sat down on the floor in front of the door. "Let me go for only an hour."
"I think the girl's gone insane!" said Sikes. "Get up, Nancy."

But Nancy refused to move. Sikes grabbed her and dragged her off to another room. There he held her captive until the church clock struck midnight and she stopped trying to escape. Leaving her to recover, he returned to Fagin.
"Why do you think she took it into her head to go out tonight?" Bill asked.
Fagin shook his head. "Woman's stubbornness, I suppose, my dear."
As he uttered these words, Nancy reappeared and took her former seat.
"It's time for me to leave," said Fagin. "Could someone bring a light so I don't fall downstairs and break my neck?"
"Show him out, Nancy," said Sikes.
Nancy followed Fagin downstairs with a candle. When they reached the front door, he turned to her and said, "What's the matter, dear?"
"What do you mean?"
Fagin whispered in her ear. "He treats you worse than he treats his dog. If you ever want revenge, come to me."
"Good night," said Nancy without showing any emotion. She shrank back as Fagin tried to pat her hand.
Fagin walked toward home, thinking about what he had just seen. "Nancy must have fallen in love with someone else," he said to himself. "That's why she's acting so strangely."

He began to think of an evil plot. If he could get Nancy to poison Sikes, that would benefit them both. She'd no longer be subjected to Sikes' cruelty. He'd no longer have to worry that Sikes might turn against him.
"The man I hate would be gone," Fagin said. "And I'd have unlimited power over Nancy because I'd know that she killed him."
But Nancy might recoil from the idea of killing Sikes. "How can I increase my influence over her?" Fagin wondered as he arrived home. And suddenly he thought of another plan.
He would send someone to spy on her and catch her with her new love. Then he could threaten to reveal this information to Sikes.
"She won't be able to refuse my request then." Fagin rubbed his hands together with glee.
The next morning Fagin was up early, waiting for a new member of his gang to appear at the breakfast table. At last the new boy, Bolter, sat down.
Fagin leaned over the table. "Bolter, I want you to do a piece of work for me that requires great care and caution."
"Is it dangerous?" Bolter looked over his cup of coffee.
"No, you only have to follow a young woman."
"I can do that," said the boy. "I was a regular sneak when I was at school. Why am I following her?"
"Just to tell me where she goes, whom she meets, and if possible what she says."
"Who is she?"
"One of us who has gone astray." Fagin got up from the table. "I'll tell you where to find her."
After that Bolter was ready to shadow the woman every day. But it was not until late Sunday night that Fagin finally summoned him to a pub.
"There," whispered Fagin. "Do you see her?"
Bolter nodded. They were hidden behind a small glass panel that enabled them to look down into a room behind the bar. After a few minutes, the woman got up and left the pub.
"Go!" Fagin nudged Bolter.
"She turned left," said one of Fagin's minions standing at the door to the pub.
Bolter stepped out into the dark street and began to follow Nancy.

It was a very dark night, and a mist hung over the river. On London Bridge two figures emerged from the mist. The woman walked quickly and looked eagerly about, as if she were searching for someone. The boy hung back in the shadows, stopping when she stopped and picking up his pace whenever she moved on.

The woman walked back and forth on the bridge. As the clocks chimed midnight, a young lady, accompanied by an old gentleman, emerged from a carriage. The woman immediately rushed up to Rose and Mr. Brownlow.
"I'm afraid to speak to you here!" said Nancy. "Follow me down these steps."
Hearing this, Bolter ran ahead of them. He bounded down the steps, which led to a landing overlooking the river. There he flattened himself against a pillar.

"This is far enough," said Mr. Brownlow, stopping partway down the dark steps but still within earshot of Bolter. "Most people would have distrusted you too much to come this far. Why not let us speak to you on the bridge, where it is light?"
"I'm afraid someone might see us," said Nancy. "I don't know why, but I have such a sense of dread tonight. I've been seeing signs of death all evening."
"It's just your imagination," Mr. Brownlow said soothingly. "We waited for you on the bridge last Sunday night. Why didn't you come?"
"I was kept away by the man that I told the lady about. I only managed to see her the first time because I slipped him a sleeping potion."
Rose gave Nancy a sympathetic look. "Speak to her kindly," Rose said to Mr. Brownlow. "The poor creature seems to need that."

"This young lady," he said, indicating Rose, "has told me everything that you communicated to her. We propose to extract the secret—whatever it may be—from this man Monks. If he won't cooperate with us, then you must hand Fagin over to us."
"Fagin!" cried Nancy, recoiling. "Never! As evil as he is and as poorly as he has treated me, I won't turn on him."
"Tell me why," said Mr. Brownlow, who did not seem surprised by this answer.
"There’s a band of us who have lived a bad life together for a long time. No one has ever turned on me, so I won't do that to any of them."
"Then put Monks into my hands and let me deal with him," Mr. Brownlow urged her.
"What if he turns against the others?" Nancy asked.
"I promise you that if the truth is forced from him, the matter will end there. Your associates will not be harmed."
Nancy did not respond for a few moments. Finally she turned back to Mr. Brownlow. "Monks will never find out that I'm the one who told you?"
"Never," vowed Mr. Brownlow. "The information will be presented to him carefully, and he will never guess where it came from."

After receiving more reassurances from both Mr. Brownlow and Rose, Nancy began to tell her story. She spoke so quietly that it was often difficult for Bolter to overhear what she was saying. After repeating the story that she had told Rose, Nancy told Mr. Brownlow where to find Monks. She described the pub where she had been earlier that night. Monks frequently went to this pub, Nancy explained, telling them when he was mostly likely to be found there.

"He's a tall man," Nancy went on. "As he walks, he constantly looks over his shoulder. He looks withered and haggard even though he can't be more than 26 or 28 years old. His lips are often discolored and disfigured with the marks of his teeth because he has desperate fits, and sometimes he even bites his hands."
"You must be well acquainted with Monks," said Mr. Brownlow.

"No. I've only seen him twice, and both times he was covered up in a large, dark cloak. I've drawn out this description from others who know him. There's one more thing," she added. "Upon his throat and sometimes visible below his neckerchief, there is—"
"A broad red mark like a burn or scald?" cried Mr. Brownlow.
"Yes!" said Nancy. "Do you know him?"
"I think I do by your description," said Mr. Brownlow. "Young woman, you've given us most valuable assistance. Now what can I do to serve you?"
"Nothing, sir," replied Nancy, weeping. "I am past all hope indeed."

"We could find you a safe hiding place in England or in another country if you fear to remain here. Before dawn you could disappear, leaving no trace. Come! I won't have you go back to your criminal associates."
"She will be persuaded now," Rose assured him.
But Nancy could not be persuaded to leave London and Bill Sikes.
"I'm chained to my old life," she explained. "I hate it, but I cannot leave. I have gone too far to turn back." She looked around quickly. "The fear comes over me again. I must go home."
